📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CD Projekt has confirmed that a physical version of The Witcher 4 will be released, even though the RPG is slated to launch after Sony Interactive Entertainment plans to stops producing physical games for PlayStation 5.
  • Sony intends to end the production of game discs for PlayStation consoles in January 2028.
  • According to recent reports, "We’re big fans of people having access to tangible collectible things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CD Projekt has confirmed that a physical version of The Witcher 4 will be released, even though the RPG is slated to launch after Sony Interactive Entertainment plans to stops producing physical games for PlayStation 5. Whether The Witcher 4 will be released on a physical disc is another matter entirely.

Sony intends to end the production of game discs for PlayStation consoles in January 2028. The Witcher 4 is the highest-profile AAA game at the moment slated to launch that year, and it comes from a studio that enjoys releasing its games physically. In an interview with The Game Business from August, CD Projekt joint CEO Michał Nowakowski confirmed that CD Projekt would still like to release a physical version of The Witcher 4.

According to recent reports, "We’re big fans of people having access to tangible collectible things. We’re nerds ourselves, and we like that. We always supported that," Nowakowski explained. "So, whatever is the case, we’re going to be for sure having a box. We’re going to have a box that’s going to have some feelies in it. Something you’re going to be wanting to open up and enjoy.".

That said, Nowakowski said he's unsure whether the game itself will be on a disc, as CD Projekt has no control over what Sony decides to manufacture. "We know what PlayStation has declared. And we have no influence on the policies of the first parties," he admitted. "The discs for the first parties, including PlayStation, have to be manufactured in their own factories. So, if they stop manufacturing indeed by 2028, then yes [we won’t have a disc].".

According to recent reports, although Nowakowski went on to tell The Game Business that he has "no influence" over whether it'll even be possible to print discs for The Witcher 4, it's good that CD Projekt is committing to a physical release regardless. That said, it's clear that PlayStation needs to better explain its intends to developers, some of whom are clearly still expressing demand for physical discs.

Industry observers note that the Witcher 4 will be released on PS5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X sometime in 2028. Before then, fans of the series can look forward to a current-generation remaster of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt on Sept. 29 and the Songs of the Past expansion for that game sometime in 2027.

Matt Damon was clearly trying to fly under the radar during an August 2026 trip to Disneyland to celebrate his daughter Gia’s 18th birthday. And the video of the movie star dad smiling as he watched and understood how special the father-daughter moment in front of him was unsurprisingly went vital.

Now Matt Damon himself has commented on the unexpected cameo appearance and the story behind it is even lovelier than I could have imagined. During an interview for The Morning Show in Canada, the star of The Odyssey (one of the biggest box office success stories on the 2026 movie schedule) explained how that sweet moment unfolding in front of him reminded him of all the moments he’d shared with his own daughter at Goofy’s Kitchen in the Disneyland Hotel. You can check out what he had to say about it in this Instagram clip:.

A post shared by Loryn Powell (@lorynpowell).

It has been revealed that when I first saw the video, I immediately thought, “Now there’s a dad who’s having a flashback of a memory with his own daughter.” So it warmed my heart to hear directly from the Good Will Hunting star that that’s exactly what happened. He, himself, has had that exact moment over the year on annual birthday trips that landed him in that very same spot.

When we think of Matt Damon, we picture the international film star, the public friendship with Ben Affleck, or even the Damon/Kimmel faux feud that started back in the early 2000s. We tend to forget that he has four daughters, which means countless family events, gatherings, birthdays, and shared experiences, and endless memories from when they were children. Being the movie star on a press tour that he is, the self-proclaimed “anti-Tom Cruise” also related it back to the movies of Christopher Nolan by saying:.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a theme in a lot of Chris’ movies, right? Of a father missing the childhood of their kids. That video, one of my kids sent that to me. Sources indicate that I love when the timing lines up and someone can ask a celebrity to explain the story behind a viral moment, making them more relatable to everyone else. And there’s nothing more human than spending and missing time with our loved ones. I can’t imagine what the family in the video thought when they realized that not only was The Bourne Identity star at Disneyland on the same day, but he was in the background of their video, reacting to that special interaction.

In a recent development, there is no shortage of celebrity sightings at theme parks, from Disney super fan Charlize Theron to John Stamos, Adam Sandler, and so many others. Something like this moment with Matt Damon makes me not only want to keep an even more keen eye out, but also comb through my own videos for anyone making an unexpected cameo appearance in the background. Especially knowing that it could lead to another sweet backstory like this one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prince William and Kate Middleton’s visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony marked their first joint overseas tour in four years, and the couple used it as an opportunity to demonstrate their star power. Through their action-packed itinerary, which took them from Mumbai to Latest Delhi, the Prince and Princess of Wales have paved the way for a new style of royal tour.

From Kate unexpectedly presenting an award and delivering a speech at the star-studded Earthshot Prize event to her and William playing cricket and traveling around Mumbai in an electric rickshaw, there have been plenty of photo opportunities and headlines around the world about the environmental initiative William is so passionate about.

Industry observers note that according to royals author Russell Myers, who followed the couple on tour, the speech Kate gave at the awards was kept top secret. “None of us knew she was presenting an award on the night, or that she was going to speak. The auditorium was packed. There were about 5,000 people there. It’s been the biggest Earthshot yet, and you could see Catherine was nervous, but she delivered an absolutely brilliant speech. I’d say her best yet.

Industry observers note that “It’s been wonderful for her to be here, supporting William, and you can see they’ve really had fun. Because of ongoing terror threats, there have been less walkabouts, but it’s been a very successful and varied tour, and I think, being shorter than most tours, it sets a fresh blueprint when it comes to royal tours for the couple in the future.”.

Prince William and Princess Kate arrive to attend the Earthshot Prize awards night at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

There are seemingly already plans for another royal tour, indicates Myers.

In a recent development, “William let slip that Australia is on the cards next, and if that’s the case, I imagine they will go as a family. They don’t want to be away from their children for too long, and what a way it would be to win support for the monarchy Down Under,” Myers indicates.

According to royals insiders, there had been some nervousness around the trip after the couple’s disastrous tour of the Caribbean in March 2022, when their visit was overshadowed by calls for the UK to apologize for slavery. Then some of their photo calls, including one that involved the couple riding in an open-top Land Rover, led to accusations of the royals appearing colonial and out of touch.

Sources indicate that “I think there has been a slight nervousness about how this tour would be received, but the reception has been really good,” Myers indicates. “The fact that William and Catherine have included a visit to Upcoming Delhi to see Prime Minister Modi is a clever move. While this is a private trip to promote Earthshot, the Foreign Office was keen for William to meet with the Indian prime minister, so they have packed that into the itinerary too.”.

It has been revealed that the visit to India has come at a time when the royals are on something of a charm offensive following a difficult year for the royal family, from Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest to what one palace insider calls “the ongoing soap opera” with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has not been charged and has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.).

William and Kate are keen to carve out their own initiatives and projects focusing on their major priorities, including the environment, children’s early years, and mental health. With the challenge of having Harry and Meghan carrying out their own engagements, the Prince and Princess of Wales have been careful to establish clear parameters that set them apart as working royals. In one telling moment while on an engagement in Mumbai, Kate was asked for an autograph. She politely declined, so as not to breach protocol, a clear contrast to the Duchess of Sussex, who has signed autographs in the past.

“Catherine was asked to sign an autograph, but she was right not to. It wasn’t a snub; it was just adhering to protocol. An autograph could be sold for money,” notes Dickie Arbiter, former press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II.

According to author Tom Bower, the royals are more relatable now than they were during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, who famously never gave a press interview. In recent weeks, Prince William has appeared as a guest on The Graham Norton Show (to promote Earthshot), and he’s revealed how he drinks his cider and his love of wild swimming as part of his guest-editing stint for a recent concern of Country Life magazine.

Industry observers note that “The royals are more relatable, perhaps, than they ever have been, but they are not celebrities. There’s a danger of being too relatable, too much ‘one of the people,’ which means they can lose some of their mystery,” Bower indicates.

Recent findings suggest that “William will have been advised to do TV appearances and take on media opportunities to bolster his public image. Of course, it’s charming to hear these nuggets and see this side of the prince, but I do think there’s a need to see and hear more from William about his broader plans. Over the years, Charles has made huge efforts to appeal to all cultural aspects of society. I’m not sure William has done that. He’s got to find a way of connecting with everyone, not just the younger generation,” Bower adds.

The Earthshot Prize awards have been a powerful way of demonstrating that William doesn’t just talk the talk; he is insisting on action.

Recent findings suggest that “The Earthshot is a master class in what needs to be done,” concludes Arbiter. “He’s pushing for environmental complications and climate change, and he’s getting people to do something about it. The fact that he is so well supported, and by so many high-profile people, shows his pulling power and influence.”.

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" adapts the story that fans have been waiting for since 2008, revealing how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor of Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), became the victor of the 50th Hunger Games. Haymitch's games were even more brutal than usual: as a special "quarter quell" game, each of the twelve districts had to offer up four children, not two. (Haymitch ends up in the games after one of the two District 12 boys originally chosen tries to flee and then is shot.).

Industry observers note that one of the District 12 kids "reaped" alongside Haymitch is Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), the daughter of a candy shop owning family. A jewelry collector, Maysilee is the original owner of the Mockingjay pin that Katniss eventually comes to wear during the "Hunger Games" trilogy.

Now, this being a prequel where Haymitch's victory (as pyrrhic as it is) is assured, you should go into "Sunrise on the Reaping" knowing Maysilee doesn't walk out of that arena. Grace actually plays two roles in the film, the other being Maysilee's twin sister, Merrilee. Once Haymitch returns, during Maysilee's funeral, he has to see the very same face of the girl he failed.

Viewers, too, might recognize Maysilee and Merrilee's shared face. Mckenna Grace is a prolific young actress with many film and TV (including voiceover) roles to her name. In just the past few years, she appeared in "Five Nights at Freddy's 2" as paranormal activity hunter Lisa, Clara in the Colleen Hoover adaptation "Regretting You," and Hannah Thurman in "Scream 7." Those recent roles only scratch the surface of her acting resume.

Born in 2006, Mckenna Grace is a recently graduated child actress; her first acting role was on the 2012 Disney XD series "Crash and Bernstein." Soon after she had a part on soap opera "The Young and the Restless" from 2013 to 2015 as Faith Newman. Her breakout film role was in 2017 Chris Evans vehicle "Gifted," where she played young math prodigy Mary Adler.

In the late 2010s, Grace found a niche playing child versions of main characters. She played young Tonya Harding in "I, Tonya," young Carol Danvers in "Captain Marvel," a young Sabrina Spellman in one episode of "The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina," and starred in Mike Flanagan's miniseries "The Haunting of Hill House" as a young version of Kate Siegel's character Theo Crain. This means she's played young versions of Margot Robbie, Brie Larson, and Kiernan Shipka. (Grace, who played Paige Swanson on sitcom "Young Sheldon," has said she envisions Reese Witherspoon as the adult version of that character.).

Recent findings suggest that from 2021 to 2022, during Seasons 4 and 5 of "The Handmaid's Tale," Grace played Esther Keyes, the abused teenage wife of a much older man. This role earned her an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Drama Series. 2021 was also the year that Grace starred in "Ghostbusters: Afterlife" as Phoebe Spangler, later reprising the role in 2024's "Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire.".

One of Grace's voiceover roles was playing a young version of Daphne Blake in the 2020 animated "Scooby Doo!" film "Scoob!" Fresh off of "Sunrise on the Reaping," she's going to play Daphne again, this time in live-action, in the upcoming TV series "Scooby Doo: Origins" due out in 2027.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is playing in theaters.

'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (483 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • According to recent reports, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's notable to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

According to recent reports, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that firm or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Recent findings suggest that next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before.
  • On one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades.
  • Industry observers note that the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unpredictable; when I went there this summer for lunch with a movie producer, we spotted a powerful name-brand media executive, an architectural bigwig who designs the homes of billionaires, and a two-time Academy Award–winning actor. A few nights later, I sat near Walter Isaacson, who’s a regular. And don’t just take it from Elon Musk’s biographer. Matthew Schneier, the chief restaurant critic at Upcoming York magazine, recently named Borgo the city’s best all-around restaurant.

On one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

Industry observers note that the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

After launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had shows recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.

As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

Industry observers note that “I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”.

The studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They highlighted figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

The studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

“It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” says Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”.

Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

Sources indicate that “I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”.

It has been revealed that he told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

“What are the processes? Like you stated, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”.

In a recent development, diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.

“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

Industry observers note that tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some upcoming development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

Industry observers note that A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few shows. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

According to recent reports, “I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”.

Sources indicate that sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

Sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”.

As a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

Recent findings suggest that “I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he noted. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”.

Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

“I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”.

According to recent reports, the show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

The showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he noted. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

“I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew noted, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy says. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”.

Like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy claims, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.

And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

“I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he stated. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”.

MobLand Season 2 Finale Delivers The Show's Most Shocking Death Yet

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article contains spoilers for "MobLand" Season 2, Episode 10, "The Queen is Dead.".
  • Just when you think the Harrigans might catch a break, things blow up in their face.
  • "Mobland" started life as a "Ray Donovan" spin-off, with Hardy set to play the English equivalent of Liev Schreiber's fixer — which he still sort of does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains spoilers for "MobLand" Season 2, Episode 10, "The Queen is Dead.".

Just when you think the Harrigans might catch a break, things blow up in their face. This time, a car literally blew up in the face of Tom Hardy's Harry Da Souza and his daughter, Gina Da Souza (Teddie Allen), during a frenetic "MobLand" Season 2 finale which almost ended without anyone kicking the bucket. In the episode's final moments, however, we witness what is surely the most shocking death in the entire series, when Joanne Froggatt's Jan Da Souza gets blown sky high thanks to Anson Boon's Eddie Harrigan.

"Mobland" started life as a "Ray Donovan" spin-off, with Hardy set to play the English equivalent of Liev Schreiber's fixer — which he still sort of does. But his Harry is much darker, colder, and quietly ruthless. Alan Ritchson once compared playing Jack Reacher to playing an alligator waiting to strike. If that's true, then Hardy's Da Souza is a human nuclear warhead, sitting at the head of a ballistic missile and waiting to reduce the world to ashes. Thus far, despite the many challenges endured by the Harrigans in "MobLand" Season 2, he's managed to maintain his icy exterior. Now that his wife has gone up in flames, however, I get the feeling that reservoir of repressed rage is going to come flooding out in Season 3.

According to recent reports, season 2, Episode 10 has a deceptive title. When I first saw "The Queen is Dead" on the Paramount+ interface, I thought Maeve Harrigan's (Helen Mirren) days were numbered. But it turns out Jan was the one to pay the piper, and if anyone was going to go down in the season finale, she was surely the least deserving.

Early on, "Mobland" Season 2 proved that it hadn't lost a step in comparison to the first run of episodes. It might even have outdone Season 1, thanks in large part to Johnny Flynn as villain Frankie Cooper, who has been a non-stop delight to watch as the flamboyant, psychopathic London gangster. But the show's been firing on all cylinders from the very first episode of Season 2, in which Pierce Brosnan's Conrad Harrigan dual-wielded his way through an entire gang at a race track.

Sources indicate that since then, we've seen the Harrigan crime family come close to collapse. A campaign of violence waged by Frankie at the behest of corrupt U.S. Ambassador Katherine "Kat" McAllister (Janet McTeer) almost wiped out the Harrigans for good. In the season finale, however, Harry Da Souza pulls off an impossibly brilliant strategy to finally oust Kat and capture Frankie, all while restoring his criminal employers to their former glory. But there's an unsettling aspect to the whole thing. By the end of the episode, nobody has died, leaving you with a sense that something truly terrible is about to happen.

The final scene sees Harry pull up to Conrad's home in the Cotswolds, leaving Jan and Gina Da Souza in the car. While Harry's inside, Gina and Jan leave the car for a chat. Meanwhile, Eddie Harrigan plants Semtex under the passenger seat and is just about to hit the detonate button when he receives a call from Colin Morgan's Kelly "Mad Dog" O'Connor. Startled, he drops the detonator just as poor old Jan gets back in the car. Boom. Harry and Gina watch the brutal scene unfold before their eyes. Eddie is surely a dead man.

Jan Da Souza's only real crime (apart from shooting Alex Fine's Donnie) has been sticking around while Harry Da Souza and his criminal cohorts engage in ever more dangerous conduct. Otherwise, she's about as innocent as a "MobLand" character can be.

According to recent reports, now, with "MobLand" Season 3 already in production, the question becomes, what sort of fallout will we see from this shocking turn of events? Surely, Eddie isn't making it out alive. The walls are already closing in on the Harrigan scion, and this cockup seals the deal.

Industry observers note that episode 5 of "MobLand" Season 2 showcased the dark side of a "Star Trek" legend when Colm Meaney portrayed an Irish gangster by the name of Medusa. Eddie was sent to kill Medusa but ultimately failed to carry out the hit, forcing Harry to finish the job. Now, Medusa's son, Mad Dog, is out for revenge. But with Eddie now having killed Jan, he'll surely face Harry's wrath, too. Can he really survive the vengeful rage of both Harry and Mad Dog?

Meanwhile, there's Gina Da Souza, who has been teetering on the verge of embracing her father's criminal life all season. Jan's death will either push her away for good or prove to be her villain origin story. It might make for a decent storyline if Harry follows through on his promise to mentor Gina and turn her into a criminal force to be reckoned with. For now, we'll have to wait to see how things play out, but it's truly exciting to see "MobLand" continuing to be the best show it can be.

#28478. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2053 w)
📖 Baca

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • It has been revealed that to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

It has been revealed that to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

Recent findings suggest that it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

In a recent development, shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This substantial-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Recent findings suggest that before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Sources indicate that horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

It has been revealed that I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

It has been revealed that alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley demonstrates up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

In a recent development, I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

Recent findings suggest that there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

According to recent reports, I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

In a recent development, I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

According to recent reports, the animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

According to recent reports, this BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

It has been revealed that A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chrissy Metz is speaking out on the latest twist on Nocturne that is hinting at a major death on the show.

During the Friday, November 20, episode of the Apple TV show, Jonah (Liev Schreiber) came to the realization that Jurek’s (Stephen Graham) kidnappings weren’t about the people who were taken. Instead, it was about hurting the people closest to them, who previously died by suicide as a result of the grief.

Sources indicate that at the same time, Ida (Metz) — who was reunited with her son after his abduction — tried to decode a message Michael (Landon Valentin) was trying to give her from the person who took him. A chilling game of hangman led to Ida realizing the mystery word was her name — as the ominous hangman hinted that Ida would need to take her own life in order to get her daughter back as well.

According to recent reports, “That’s what’s so petrifying about Jurek is that he doesn’t do the killing. The people do it to themselves,” Metz, 46, explained about the psychological warfare during an exclusive interview with Us. “It’s a lot.”.

Metz called the reveal “beyond chilling and scary and sad and just devastating.”.

“Nothing is really stronger than a mother’s love and I think that at that point she’s prepared to do whatever he asks of her and to keep her children safe,” she said about Us‘ concern for Ida moving forward. “I think you got that right.”.

Recent findings suggest that nocturne follows a former homicide detective who relocates to a small Pennsylvania town, which comes under attack by an imprisoned serial killer. At the center of the case is Ida’s family, who is reeling from the return of her son — but also her daughter’s ongoing disappearance.

In a recent development, while Metz told Us she would love another season, she remained more tight-lipped about whether Ida could actually return, adding, “It was wonderful to work with everybody and they’re obviously so talented and it was really wonderful to watch a master class of actors. Should you be worried? Yes, I think you should be a little worried.”.

She continued: “There’s some things that will transpire that I think will be shocking and I know for me it’s something that I’ve never done in any role before, which was concerning for Stephen [Graham] and Liev, who were like, ‘Are you sure?’ And I’m like, ‘This is not real.'”.

Metz hinted that the story lines evolved.

Industry observers note that “They were sort of campaigning for us to do something different but it is shocking. It’s scary,” she told Us. “It is very intense. Something very different.”.

While reflecting on the role, Metz also discussed getting the chance to depict such a rich story.

It has been revealed that “I always say that women aren’t depicted on screen enough. The stories are just not told enough. I’m so glad that they made her a woman [since she is a man in the book] and a mother. She is a regular woman just trying to survive as a single mom and I know that story very well because my mom was a single mom and raised children on her own,” she told Us. “I know what it’s like to sort of live paycheck to paycheck, and hope that you have enough for bills and to put food on the table. So I gravitate toward those those women and those characters and the stories because they don’t get told enough. I think people need to feel seen and heard in any way and that’s what’s brilliant about art and TV and film.”.

Nocturne airs upcoming episodes Fridays on Apple TV.

  • As per old research by the now-defunct website The Silph Road (via Wayback Machine), shiny rates on Community Days are about 1 in 24, which means that if you keep playing throughout the three-hour window, you should find quite a few shiny Pokémon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pokémon Go is having a Pawniard Community Day event on Saturday, Nov. 21 from 2-5 p.m. in your local time. This event is indeed running alongside the "Dynamax Trails" event, and it begins right when Eternatus' stint in the morning ends.

Sources indicate that as expected with a Community Day event, Pawniward will spawn in huge numbers with a high chance for it to appear shiny. There are also several other bonuses and perks, which we've listed out below.

As per old research by the now-defunct website The Silph Road (via Wayback Machine), shiny rates on Community Days are about 1 in 24, which means that if you keep playing throughout the three-hour window, you should find quite a few shiny Pokémon.

If you’re short on time or Poké Balls, you can pop an Incense, then promptly tap each Pawniard to check for shiny ones, running from any that aren’t shiny. Notably, any Pawniard you’ve already tapped will face where your player is standing, so that should help identify which ones you may have already checked.

In a recent development, if you evolve Bisharp into Kingambit from 2-9 p.m. in your local time, it will learn the charged move Kowtow Cleave.

According to recent reports, if you miss out on evolving it during this period, you will likely be able to evolve it during a Community Day weekend event in December to get Kowtow Cleave. If you don’t want to wait, you can use an Elite TM to get the move.

In a recent development, usually, to evolve Bisharp into Kingambit, you'd need to set Bisharp as your buddy and beat 15 dark- or steel-type Pokémon in raids. However, for this Community Day, this requirement has been reduced heavily.

Industry observers note that on Saturday, Nov. 21 from 2-9 p.m., you will only need to defeat 1 dark- or steel-type Pokémon in a raid with Bisharp as your buddy to evolve it into Kingambit. The evolution will still cost 100 Pawniard Candy, though. The Bisharp you are trying to evolve won't need to be used in the raid, it just needs to be set as your buddy Pokémon.

With its Community Day move, Kingambit is actually a very strong dark-type attacker, only falling to Mega and shadow Pokémon. Definitely power one up and give it Snarl and Kowtow Cleave for success.

In a recent development, its Community Day move also makes it a strong pick in PvP, specifically in the Great League. Run it with Low Kick, Iron Head, and Kowtow Cleave to make the most of it.

The following bonuses will be active during Pawniard Community Day:.

That said, you should definitely put your eggs in Incubators and pop an Incense and try to nab some powerful Pawniard.

If you can Mega Evolve Gyarados, Steelix, Scizor, Skarmory, Houndoom, Tyranitar, Sableye, Mawile, Aggron, Sharpedo, Absol, Metagross, Lucario, Greninja, or Malamar, you’ll score additional Pawniard Candy per catch.

Just the same as previous Community Days this year, the Lure Module bonus will be active for this event, too. Pawniard will continue to spawn from Lure Modules placed until 9 p.m., retaining their Community Day shiny rate and their chance to spawn with a Special Background.

This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

In a recent development, it’s True Colors, from New York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

In a recent development, one thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in New York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

According to recent reports, speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

Industry observers note that we’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this concern: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian.

Recent findings suggest that van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

Honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

So who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is currently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

The $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

It has been revealed that — As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

The 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

— Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

Sources indicate that — The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred mentioned the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”.

Sources indicate that — For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

Industry observers note that — Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

— After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

— The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.

On a Friday in November, I walk into Gagosian on Madison Avenue for a meeting with Michael Chow, the artist, collector, filmmaker, designer, actor, and founder of the restaurant Mr. Chow. There’s a portrait of Chow by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a portrait by Julian Schnabel, a portrait by Andy Warhol. There’s a drawing of Chow by David Hockney, made soon after Mr. Chow opened in London in 1968.

Michael Chow: So I opened that restaurant. You’ve got Hockney, you’ve got fashion, you’ve got every single thing. It’s almost like a Dada movement on the First World War thing. This one is in London—all happening.

It has been revealed that he starts talking about duopolys: Christie’s versus Sotheby’s, Coke versus Pepsi. There was an Italian restaurant in London’s Soho, so he opened a Chinese restaurant in Soho with Italian waiters. He has a theory about name-dropping.

Chow: I hate people who drop names, and Lady Gaga agrees with me.

True Colors: That’s a good one.

Why is name-dropping important? Because the minute I say “Napoleon,” you will go there immediately. So it saves a lot of time. Okay, so why am I saying that? Do you know who Robert Fraser is?

The art dealer from the ’60s. Groovy Bob.

It has been revealed that I was looking forward to meeting him, blah, blah, blah. He was sitting there. Name-dropping. Sitting in front is Jim Dine. Name-dropping again. I say, “I would like to borrow some paintings.” I said, “Just like”—do you know the Kronenhalle restaurant?

We walk over to the Hockney portrait of Michael Chow sitting in his restaurant.

According to recent reports, chow: The first person I went to is David. He drew one and I said, “Boy.” You know what he did? Tore it all up.

According to recent reports, simultaneously, I went to Peter Blake. I say, “Give me a painting that’s the antithesis of racism,” which he did. At that time he’s into the circus, he’s into all that shit. All right? So I asked him, “Why did you do that?” He did a portrait. So now Peter Blake is fucking crazy. He loves the circus, he loves wrestling and all that shit.

Industry observers note that larry Gagosian walks in and gives Chow a fist bump. Gagosian takes a long look at the Schnabel and then flips through a book of drawings made by artists for 57th Street’s Mr. Chow when it was the art world’s clubhouse. We walk up to the Basquiat.

Industry observers note that true Colors: To have it as this sort of landscape, you have the horizon line here, but it’s almost like a Western. It’s almost cinematic.

Chow: Name me three classic Westerns.

Shane. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. High Noon.

I’m going to act out the first scene of each. Okay, High Noon.

He uses his hand to pull a finger gun on me, then gets distracted by the Ed Ruscha and the Warhol double portrait.

Chow: Andy noted, “Oh, what do you want?” I said, “Hold the color and add lots of diamonds.”.

Gagosian brings up Anselm Kiefer, and then Richard Serra.

Chow: If you look at the year 2000, Charlie Rose and Richard Serra, their conversation on the culture of China, and Richard Serra identifies very clearly what is fine art: poetry, music, sculpture, and painting.

The works in the show are for sale. I ask Chow if he’s emotional about parting with them. He seems very calm.

Chow: I’m only a temporary steward of the works.

“Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow” is up at Gagosian’s 980 Madison space until December 22.

Breaking: Why The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Is The Darkest Movie In The Series

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The following post contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".
  • Sources indicate that it's rare for a franchise to get better after 4 or 5 movies, especially when they are prequels that explore questions no one needed answered.
  • And yet, when it comes to "Hunger Games," not only has the franchise improved with time, but the two spin-off prequels are arguably better than even the original series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The following post contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

Sources indicate that it's rare for a franchise to get better after 4 or 5 movies, especially when they are prequels that explore questions no one needed answered. It didn't work for "Star Wars," it didn't work for "Harry Potter," and it shouldn't work for "Hunger Games." At best, these prequels just introduced characters that don't matter in the large scheme of things because everything they do or accomplish gets erased in the original story, at worst they try so hard to answer questions no one cares about that it ends up tarnishing the original work.

And yet, when it comes to "Hunger Games," not only has the franchise improved with time, but the two spin-off prequels are arguably better than even the original series. The latest film, "Sunrise on the Reaping" deepens what came before, while introducing new characters that are as engaging as those we know and add to the larger worldbuilding of Panem. Or, as /Film's review puts it, "Beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end.".

Even if this movie doesn't have the compelling romance that was central to "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," it delivers a harrowing tale of rebellion. What's more, this is somehow the darkest movie in the "Hunger Games" series, and it's not even close. Not just in terms of deaths — though there are some truly brutal deaths in the movie (which are somehow tamer than the book!) — but also in the overall tone the movie explores. This is the "Hunger Games" equivalent of "Andor" or "Rogue One," a bleak tragedy about one man who dared stand up against a tyrannical government and paid for it with everything he had.

It has been revealed that the "Hunger Games" movies are full of death and suffering; it's part of the game. But "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes it to another level. Though it takes a long while before the nearly 3-hour runtime gets to the actual games, there's a feeling of hopelessness from the first moment. Early on, a kid gets shot for trying to escape the Reaping. Later, on the day of the opening ceremony, the youngest tribute from District 12, Loella, gets brutally killed in a chariot accident.

But it's not just the fact that there are plenty of deaths, or that they're horrible to watch. Sure, seeing poor Ampert get completely mauled by a swarm of cute forest animals and Maysilee Donner getting gored to death by birds is harrowing. The Capitol doesn't just kill children; it tortures them and pulls them apart and makes their parents watch.

In a recent development, indeed, more than the deaths themselves, it's the meanness around them that makes this movie stand out. When Loella dies, it isn't a murder done by another tribute trying to get an advantage. Instead, it's an accident caused by Capitol audiences throwing flares at the parade circuit knowing full well it will cause the chariot horses to go berserk, because they want to see the tributes suffer. Compared to every other "Hunger Games" movie, the tributes are not only livestock sent to slaughter, or pawns in a political game. Here, they are subjects of absolute torture, playthings to be slowly toyed with and brutalized before getting discarded for the pleasure of others.

In a recent development, we especially see this in the presence of Ampert, whom we learn is only in the games as a punishment for his father Beetee's rebellious activities. Beetee is forced to mentor his own son and then watch him die.

It has been revealed that throughout "Sunrise on the Reaping," there is a sense of hopelessness and inevitability. We know that, eventually, the Hunger Games end and the Capitol falls — but the characters in the movie don't know that. At every turn, Haymitch and his allies see their every effort get squashed and mocked. Their attempts at leveling the playfield just a little bit are met with overwhelming force. Even before the games begin, Haymitch knows he'll never get to go back home because President Snow has personally seen to it that Haymitch dies for his insubordination during the opening ceremony.

It has been revealed that then we get to the third act, where the movie just becomes a cruel feel-bad experience, as Plutarch Heavensbee convinces Snow to let Haymitch survive to prolong his suffering. Haymitch is forced to watch Maysilee die brutally at the hands of waterbird mutts while he is virtually unscathed. Then, even after he wins the games, Haymitch discovers that the televised games were heavily edited to make him look selfish and cowardly, a traitor to every one of his allies, who won only because he was lucky. As if that wasn't enough, Haymitch has to see his family and his girlfriend die horrible deaths after he goes back home from the death games, in what's without a doubt the most nihilistic ending in the franchise.

Industry observers note that it makes sense, however. "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place at a pivotal moment in the "Hunger Games" timeline, at the height of President Snow's power. We are far removed from the games being almost canceled due to lack of interest like in the previous movie, but also far removed from the simmering rebellion of the original movies. Here, Snow gets away with everything, and he relishes in the cruelty of his games.
