  • In a recent development, gone are the golden years of cable TV, when viewers could expect their favorite highlights to return year after year without fail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, julio is a Senior Author for Collider. He studied History and International Relations at university, but found his calling in cultural journalism. When he isn't writing, Julio also teaches English at a nearby school. He has lived in São Paulo most of his life, where he covers CCXP and other significant events. Having loved movies, music, and TV from an early age, he prides himself in knowing every minute detail about the things he loves. When he is older, he dreams of owning a movie theater in a small countryside town.

In a recent development, the best news for fans of spy thrillers this week isn't what you'd expect. While everyone was celebrating a newly introduced James Bond, MI5 actually had the biggest shake-up as Apple TV announced the renewal of Slow Horses for Seasons 9 and 10. You read that right — Season 6 has barely wrapped up, and viewers can already look forward to four more seasons of Jackson Lamb's (Gary Oldman) trademark grumpiness. This comes as a great surprise, not just the number of seasons itself, but given the greater circumstances. Back in September, Apple had already renewed Slow Horses for Season 8, and now, less than two months later, has confirmed an incredible Season 10 update. It's a really unprecedented move for any streamer, so is there a catch — or are things just that good at Slough House?

In a recent development, gone are the golden years of cable TV, when viewers could expect their favorite highlights to return year after year without fail. Getting lost in series like Friends, Supernatural, and Grey's Anatomy was a pleasure, but, with the dawn of the streaming age, it became harder and harder to find such long-running shows — so much so that people usually point to these behemoths of old when looking for long-term commitment on TV, as those titles remain available on most streaming platforms.

It has been revealed that because of the usual budget constraints, long-term casting commitments, and ever-changing business models, scripted live-action highlights rarely go beyond six or seven seasons on streaming, so Slow Horses earning this type of renewal is completely unprecedented in the current landscape. Its now-confirmed 10-season run makes it Apple TV's longest-running series — a title it previously shared with For All Mankind, which is slated to end with Season 6.

Recent findings suggest that there are a few reasons that have resulted in Slow Horses getting this kind of treatment. Each season has only six episodes, making it much quicker to produce, and every season finale delivers a preview for the next batch of episodes. Most crucial, though, is how well it performs among audiences and critics. On Rotten Tomatoes, every season of Slow Horses has consistently performed above 95%, so, from a business perspective, what's not to love about it?

Sources indicate that on its own, this unexpected renewal is bound to keep Slow Horses and Apple TV at the top of viewers' minds for a while, especially with a upcoming season set to premiere next year. Its consistent release schedule is another reason this series has performed so well since the beginning. (Longer gaps between seasons are another streaming staple, unfortunately.) To keep the pace, a quick production is important, but what's really vital is the fact that there has always been source material available to adapt for each new season.

In a recent development, slow Horses famously adapts Mick Herron's Slough House book series, which currently comprises nine entries. From the beginning, each season has adapted one book, with the exception being Season 6 — which adapted two novels, Joe Country and Slough House. Right now, the expectation is that Season 7 will adapt Bad Actors and Season 8 will adapt Clown Town, Herron's most recent novel published in 2025.

Sources indicate that now that Slow Horses has been renewed for more, though, Seasons 9 and 10 don't yet have a published Herron novel to adapt — at least for now. The expectation is that a tenth Slough House novel will be announced, although there has been no confirmation as of this writing. Herron has previously mentioned that he already knows "why, when, and where Jackson Lamb dies," so it stands to reason that the Apple TV series won't run forever, and its end may be steadily approaching.

Sources indicate that even if Herron's tenth novel takes longer to reach publication than anticipated, there are still five Slough House novellas for the show to draw from, all compiled in Watch the Quiet Snow. It's still way too early to know where Slow Horses is headed in Seasons 9 and 10, but it seems unlikely that Apple TV would take such a bold step in renewing it without a clear proposal.

Curiously, the timing of this renewal news couldn't have been better. Mere days prior, Olivia Cooke, who plays Sidonie "Sid" Baker, said in an interview that Season 8 would be Slow Horses' last, even mentioning that the cast has been "all melancholy" while filming. Apple TV's renewal immediately refutes this, adding another two seasons to the previously confirmed seventh and eighth back in September. (Hopefully, Season 8 isn't Cooke's last season, though.).

Sources indicate that finally, there is the "James Bond" of it all. Jack Lowden, who plays down-on-his-luck protagonist River Cartwright, was among the top contenders for 007, but although fans rooted for him until the very end, the role ultimately went to Robert Pattinson. Ironically, hoping to get out of Slough House for a better position in a government agency only to ultimately get shot down is such a Cartwright thing that we can almost hear Lamb laughing in the background. So far, only Oldman's return has been confirmed, but it's hard to imagine Slow Horses without the rest of Lamb's joes, no matter how many seasons the show ultimately runs for.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's almost Thanksgiving, and as you prepare to fly home (well, depending on if planes are allowed in the sky when you need to do that), you might be feeling a weird sense of dread about sleeping in your parent's house next to their dusty Peloton on your old Spider-Man sheets. Why not binge-watch some stuff to deal with those feelings?

In a recent development, I've got you covered. There's a handful of upcoming releases coming to major streaming platforms this week, and honestly? This is a pretty good handful. While major titles like "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" captivate people who decide to head to a movie theater and hang out there for a few hours, maybe you're looking for a scenario where you don't have to wear real pants and can pause whatever you're watching whenever the fancy strikes you. From one of the biggest horror hits in recent memory to the final season of a mystery box series to an offbeat biopic helmed by a Canadian comedy favorite, here are five movies or demonstrates to stream on Netflix, Disney+, Paramount+, Peacock, or HBO Max over November 20-22, 2026.

Besides the creepypasta horror hit "Backrooms," "Obsession" is the other film credited with keeping the horror genre young and fresh in 2026 — and it's not just because Kane Parsons and Curry Barker, the respective directors of those films, were born in 2005 and 1999. (As someone born in 1990, I admittedly do think about that a lot.) "Obsession," which is now available to watch on Netflix, and was completely devised by Barker, tells the story of Baron "Bear" Bailey (Michael Johnston), a young man carrying a torch for his platonic friend Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette, who may just end up earning an Oscar nod in 2027). After using a weird artifact called the One Wish Willow that he finds at an oddities store trying to get Nikki a gift, Bear wishes that Nikki would love him more than anything in the world ... and boy, does he get his wish.

Not only does Nikki really love Bear after the One Wish Willow takes effect, she seems unable to leave his side or focus on anything else — as if she's under some sort of hypnotic spell. "Obsession" is a dark, unsettling, and tightly directed horror film that interrogates Nikki's agency, Bear's distinct role in his own downfall, and what happens when you want someone to love you without actually knowing how they feel in the first place. "Obsession" is innovative, compelling, and one of the most popular movies in recent memory — and now, it's on Netflix.

When we last saw the titular Yellowjackets — a teenage soccer team stranded in the Canadian wilderness after a plane crash nearly two years prior — during the Showtime series' penultimate season in 2025, the teenagers in that wilderness were on the precipice of being rescued in the late 1990s. Meanwhile, in the more modern timeline, their adult counterparts are still trying to cover up whatever happened out in those woods. Now, in the fourth and final season (which earned a solid review right here at /Film), there are three timelines: one where the teenagers finish out their time in the wilderness, one after they've been rescued and dropped back into their "normal" lives in Upcoming Jersey, and that adult one, where all hell threatens to break loose as Shauna Shipman (Melanie Lynskey) continues to break bad after absolutely losing her s**t in Season 3.

Industry observers note that jasmin Savoy Brown, Liv Hewson, Sophie Thatcher, Sammi Hanratty, Courtney Eaton, and Sophie Nélisse make up the core of the teenage cast, while in the adult one, the always wonderful Lynskey is joined by Tawny Cypress, Christina Ricci, and even Oscar winner Hilary Swank (after former adult actors Lauren Ambrose, Juliette Lewis, and Simone Kessell exited at various points, though it's easy to imagine that they could reappear in Season 4 flashbacks at some point). As someone who's been watching this puzzle box show since the very beginning, I'll admit I have substantive doubts about "Yellowjackets" landing the plane (and it's not like its track record with these things is pretty great, if you consider the pun), but I'll definitely be watching Season 4 following its premiere on Paramount+ with Showtime on November 20, with upcoming episodes airing weekly.

Recent findings suggest that to call "Tony" a biopic feels ... sort of misleading. Directed by Matt Johnson (who recently wowed comedy nerds, a term I use affectionately, with "Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie" and cut his teeth on another biopic of sorts, "Blackberry"), the film follows a young Anthony Bourdain, played by the wry, excellent Dominic Sessa, as he learns a thing or two about life and proper oyster-shucking technique during a fateful summer in Providence, Rhode Island. Alongside a chef who never gets a proper name (Antonio Banderas) and who owns a small seafood place called "The Flagship," the titular Tony, who keeps insisting he's not an aspiring culinary expert but a writer with a fellowship (not true), pursues the girl of his dreams — photographer Nancy (Emilia Jones) — and gets into trouble with his fellow chef Sal (Leo Woodall) as he tries to figure out who he is and what he wants out of this experience.

I didn't love "Tony" as much as many of my peers (see: /Film's own Bill Bria's review of the movie), but if you mentally remove the Bourdain of it all from the film and enjoy it as a showcase for Sessa's talents and Johnson's comedic timing, you'll probably get way more mileage out of this fresh, generally fun film. "Tony" is on HBO Max now, which makes sense, as its studio, A24, tends to premiere its movies there when they come to streaming.

It has been revealed that author Rick Riordan co-created the Disney+ series "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" for Disney+ along with Jonathan E. Steinberg ("Jericho"), and whether you're a fan of Riordan's original books, enjoyed the short-lived "Percy Jackson" film franchise, or have been waiting for this show to return since Season 2 concluded back in January of 2026, you'll be happy to hear that Season 3 premiered on Disney+ on November 20. In the inaugural season released in late 2023, the action follows the plot of Riordan's novel "The Lightning Thief" and sees the titular Percy, played by Walker Scobell, discovering that not only are Greek gods real, he has magical powers and can learn how to wield them at a place called Camp Half-Blood. After using the Empire State Building to reach Olympus at the end of Season 1, Season 2 catches up with Percy during the events of Riordan's book "The Sea of Monsters," which brings a bunch of elements of "The Odyssey" into play.

Recent findings suggest that so, what about Season 3? It's set to follow Riordan's third novel, "The Titan's Curse," where Percy has to face off against Kronos and his army to rescue the goddess Artemis (Dafne Keen) and his friend Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries). The first two episodes of Season 3 dropped on Disney+ on November 20, with two episodes debuting every Friday throughout its run.

"Alien: Romulus" came out in 2024, and now, it's available to stream on Peacock. Fede Álvarez's entry into the storied "Alien" franchise features tons of rising stars like Cailee Spaeny, David Jonsson (who's gearing up to play the son of the late "Black Panther" star Chadwick Boseman's T'Challa in the Marvel Cinematic Universe), Spike Fearn, and Isabela Merced, and as it unfolds, we see half a dozen young colonists trying to navigate the deep recesses of space and finding dangerous creatures inside of an old space station. As orphan Marie Raines "Rain" Carradine (Spaeny) gathers the crew, including her adopted android brother Andy (Jonsson), her ex-boyfriend Tyler (Archie Renaux), his pregnant sister Kay (Merced), their cousin Bjorn (Fearn), and his adoptive sister Navarro (Aileen Wu), they encounter enemies left and right, leaving them shaken and fighting for their lives as they try to reach safety.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to "Alien" movies, mileage may vary, but "Romulus" is a legitimately great entry to the property. (Just look at that unbelievable cast!) It's also streaming on Peacock now, so the movie can creep you out from the comfort of your own home.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are always going to be a massive number of deaths in any Hunger Games movie, as that is simply the nature of the franchise.
  • Adding to that number, though, were two deaths that take place before the Games even begin and several that take place afterward, all having to do with punishing Haymich Abernathy for his rebellious behavior in the Games.
  • Recent findings suggest that woodbine Chance is the first death in Sunrise on the Reaping, and he is actually why Haymitch ends up in the Hunger Games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are always going to be a massive number of deaths in any Hunger Games movie, as that is simply the nature of the franchise. However, the newest installment, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, actually has significantly more deaths than the prior Hunger Games movies (except The Mockinjay - Part 2 when there is an all-out war, but those many deaths are largely not depicted on screen) because this Hunger Games is the Second Quarter Quell, in which 48 told tributes were reaped. Given that, there were always going to be, at minimum, 47 deaths in this Hunger Games.

Adding to that number, though, were two deaths that take place before the Games even begin and several that take place afterward, all having to do with punishing Haymich Abernathy for his rebellious behavior in the Games. However, unlike in the book, most of the tributes go unnamed and/or get very little screen time. By the first fight's conclusion in the arena, in fact, 20 are already dead. With so many deaths, many of which occur off screen and are never extrapolated upon, there are really just 12 key deaths that happen in the movie. Here's how each of those major characters die before the end of Sunrise on the Reaping.

Recent findings suggest that woodbine Chance is the first death in Sunrise on the Reaping, and he is actually why Haymitch ends up in the Hunger Games. Woodbine is the final name called during District 12's Reaping, but he decides to run off rather than be taken to the Capitol for the Games. As a result, he is immediately shot, leading his mother to run to him. In a devastating scene, Lenore Dove tries to interfere on the mother's behalf, and when Peacekeepers go to attack her, Haymitch steps in. Because of this, he is made Woodbine's replacement in the Hunger Games.

Louella, or Haymitch's "sweetheart," as she's also called, has a tragic death, despite her never entering the arena. Specifically, just as in the book, in the movie, Louella dies as a result of an accident during the chariot ride, wherein the horses become scarred from objects being tossed onto the track and ultimately run off, crashing into other chariots. In the book, Haymitch is described as being drenched in her blood, but the movie is not nearly as graphic. Still, her death leads to Haymitch doing his clap in front of President Snow—his first open sign of defiance that seals his fate.

The second District 12 tribute to die is Wyatt Callow, the boy whose family has made enemies in the district because they take bets on the Hunger Games. However, he eventually wins over his fellow District 12 tributes, and it's gutting that he dies, especially because it happens so early in the Games. In the book, Haymitch doesn't see this transpire, but he later learns that Wyatt died trying to protect Lou Lou. In the movie, audiences actually see Silka kill Wyatt as he runs to defend Lou Lou (who does get away, although her death soon follows).

In a recent development, it was always clear that Lou Lou was going to die in the arena, but the remaining District 12 tributes at least wanted to keep her as safe as they could and, ideally, prevent a death that was too painful. Ultimately, Lou Lou dies because she breathes in poisonous pollen from the plants in the arena. There is a slight change between how this is done in the movie and how this is done in the book, though. In the book, Lou Lou has a pump attached to her that sends drugs into her as the Capitol sees fit. Haymitch uses this to mercy kill her in the book. In the movie, he instead watches as she dies.

Ampert's death is absolutely devastating, especially because it's established that he was put in the arena (and marked for death) in order to punish his father, Beetee. Beetee even tells Haymitch earlier in the movie that he knows Ampert is doomed to die, and he simply asks that Haymitch not allow him to suffer. Unfortunately, try as Haymitch might, Ampert does suffer before his crushing death, as he's swarmed by ravenous squirrels who essentially eat him. In the book, he's described as being only a skeleton, whereas in the movie, he's gravely injured by the squirrels but he does not lose his skin.

Panache long seemed like the greatest threat in the arena, and he and Silka no doubt were, but Panache is taken down before multiple other characters. After an altercation between Haymitch and two other tributes, during which Haymitch actually takes them both out, Panache moves to kill Haymitch. Thankfully, Maysilee is nearby and uses poisoned darts to shoot Panache from afar, leading to his death. In the book, it's revealed that Maysilee actually fashioned the poisoned darts herself, using poisoned berries she found in the arena, although in the movie, that detail is left out.

Easily one of the saddest deaths in Sunrise on the Reaping is that of Maysilee Donner, who becomes a sister to Haymitch throughout their time in the arena. In the book, Maysilee's death comes about in large part due to her decision to kill Gamemakers who enter the arena during the Hunger Games. However, the movie doesn't show that scene, instead positioning her death as something that happens to punish Haymitch. In either case, though, Maysilee dies after a pack of vicious birds swarm, ultimately pecking her to death as Haymitch helplessly looks on.

Sources indicate that in both the book and the movie, Wellie is one of the Newcomers, making her an ally to Haymitch Abernathy. In fact, in the book, Haymitch even actively hopes that she is going to be the victor after Maysilee dies. Sadly, that isn't ultimately Wellie's fate. Instead, she is killed by Silka as one of the final deaths in the arena. In the book, this is actually all the more horrifying, as Silka actually decapitates Wellie and then holds up her head. In the movie, Silka is still the one to kill Wellie, but she does so off-screen, using Wellie's bell to lure Haymitch to where they are.

Silka is one of the other ruthless, incredibly dangerous careers (although, notably, her story is one of the many changes in Sunrise on the Reaping, as she's actually shown crying in the book, but that was cut out of the movie), and she becomes the final person standing other than Haymitch. The two have one final fight, in which it seems like Silka is going to win—at least, it would, if audiences didn't already know that Haymitch is the victor—as she cuts a deep gash in Haymitch's stomach. However, when she throws her axe at Haymitch, he is able to use the force field to his advantage, sending the axe flying back at her, killing her.

Industry observers note that although Sunrise on the Reaping contains many heartbreaking deaths, there are perhaps few, if any, more gutting than the deaths of Ma and Sid because it is just outright cruelty, hatred, and proof that President Snow will do whatever he wants that lead to their deaths. Specifically, after surviving the arena, Haymitch finally makes his way home to District 12, only to discover his home engulfed in flames. He tries desperately to run to Sid and his Ma, but he's held back and informed that it's too late. In the end, Sid and Ma are buried in one casket, as they were found holding onto each other.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A smoke break at the Signature Theatre ultimately resulted in one of Lois Smith‘s most fascinating performances. The Tony Award winner met Zane Pais while they were both grabbing a quick cigarette while rehearsing plays. Pais had been an admirer of Smith’s work in stage productions like “The Inheritance” and films such as “Marjorie Prime” and “Five Easy Pieces,” and longed to collaborate.

“She has the most amazing delivery of lines; she’s always able to do something so unexpected with the language,” Pais said during a recent Zoom interview with Smith. “I’ve seen Lois my whole life in so many amazing highlights, just be so unbelievably present on stage and be such a generous actor, and just give these heartfelt and unexpected performances. I’m a big fucking fan.” Related Stories Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio? Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear.

In a recent development, so Pais wrote a short film, “Lightning Bug,” with Smith in mind. In it, she plays Lydia, a fiercely independent nonagenarian who is being pressured into selling the family home by her son and granddaughter. But things take an unexpected turn when a strange young man crashes their dinner, giving Lydia a chance to demonstrate she hasn’t missed a step despite her advanced age.

“It was all there in the script,” Smith, who recently turned 96, said. “It wasn’t complex for me to pull it off even though the script is complex.”.

The role did require Smith to perform some fight choreography, but she seemed more nervous about singing a song on screen.

“I really worried: Am I going to be able to do this?” Smith said. “They made me a tape, and I listened to it and listened to it and practiced. I was nervous, but it went all right.”.

It has been revealed that “Lightning Bug” filmed over a weekend in the upstate Fresh York home of one of Pais’s relatives. It was true no-frills, all-hands effort. The cast and crew bunked in an Airbnb, and a friend of Pais’s cooked meals for everyone.

“It felt like we were part of a theater troupe,” Pais noted. “We’d work hard. Then in the evenings, we would have red wine and smoke cigarettes.”.

“I seldom smoke,” Smith interjected. “Occasionally, I’ll smoke other people’s cigarettes.”.

In a recent development, “Lightning Bug” has won awards on the festival circuit and is Academy Awards eligible this season. The film also stars Bubba Weiler, Josh Hamilton, and Anna Baryshnikov. Here’s the full short:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most of the conversation around iOS 27 was centered on Apple’s upgraded, AI-powered Siri, which brings deeper on-screen awareness and smarter multi-step actions. The catch is that Apple Intelligence requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, leaving anyone holding onto an older compatible handset locked out of the headline feature.

In a recent development, if you have been putting off the enhancement assuming there is nothing in it for older hardware, it is worth reconsidering. Beneath the AI marketing, Apple rolled out several high-impact security, camera, and interface upgrades that run without Apple Intelligence — and these three additions make a meaningful difference in daily use.

Industry observers note that scammers frequently rely on high-pressure calls and spoofed texts to trick you into wiring funds or surrendering credentials. Introduced in iOS 27, Impersonation Risk Detection serves as Apple’s built-in defense against this social engineering, and it works without requiring Apple Intelligence.

To activate it, open Settings, tap Privacy & Security, scroll down and select Impersonation Risk Detection, then toggle it on.

Industry observers note that the system monitors on-device interaction patterns and behavioral cues during high-stakes actions without reading your personal messages, emails, or photos. If you attempt a large transfer or sensitive account change under signs of coercion, your iPhone flags the event and directs supported banking apps to require secondary verification before funds can leave your account.

According to recent reports, over the last few iOS updates, Apple has tucked more manual toggles behind the Camera app’s six-dot menu, adding extra taps whenever you want to tweak exposure, aspect ratio, or timer settings before taking a shot. iOS 27 fixes that friction by letting you pin your essential controls directly to the top of the viewfinder.

Launch the Camera app, tap the six-dot icon and hit Edit in the top-left corner. From there, tap any highlighted tools you want kept within thumb’s reach, remove shortcuts you rarely touch using the minus badge, and tap Done.

Even better, iOS 27 saves separate pinned layouts per shooting mode, allowing you to tailor your quick-access toolbar individually for Photo, Portrait, Video, Cinematic, Slow-Mo, and Time-Lapse.

Sources indicate that apple’s translucent Liquid Glass design has remained one of iOS’s most polarizing visual shifts since its debut, particularly when semi-transparent menus sit over bright or busy wallpapers. Rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all look, iOS 27 introduces a dedicated precision slider so you can tailor how much transparency appears across your system interface.

Open Settings, tap Appearance, and select Liquid Glass to find the upcoming control. Sliding the toggle to the left preserves the full see-through glass aesthetic, while moving it to the right applies a heavier, tinted backdrop that makes buttons and text significantly easier to read at a glance.

A live preview window sits directly above the slider so you can test the contrast before locking in your preferred look.

#28466. Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’

Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived).
  • “The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts.
  • In a recent development, “ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived). On Wednesday night, Hill spoke before a packed screening at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and looked back on the movie that jump-started not only his screenwriting endeavors, but a directing career that would ultimately include classics like “The Warriors,” “48hrs.,” and “Streets of Fire.” Related Stories Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here Is A24 Finally Significant Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

“The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts. “The Getaway” was, appropriately enough, selected by the writers branch, and screenwriter and Academy Governor Larry Karaszewski was on hand to introduce the movie and moderate the pre-screening discussion with Hill. Karaszewski, a longtime “Getaway” enthusiast who carried newspaper ads from the movie around in his wallet when he was 10 years old, pointed out that Hill changed the entire architecture of screenwriting when he burst onto the scene in the early 1970s.

In a recent development, “ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski mentioned. “We have an award show here at the Oscars called the Sci-Tech Awards, where they give awards to things that silently change the industry and advance them into the future. I really feel that Walter Hill did that in screenwriting, but it wasn’t a technical advancement. It was a literary advancement. He changed what a page should look like as a screenplay and what it could feel like to read it.” Karaszewski went on to illustrate his point by projecting pages from Robert Bolt’s “Doctor Zhivago” screenplay and Walter Hill’s “Hard Times” side by side on the screen.

Sources indicate that “You don’t even have to read [Bolt’s script], just look at it,” Karaszewski stated, pointing out the dense blocks of words compared to Hill’s lean, spare page. “You’re looking at monoliths. It’s dense, and there are camera moves and references to things you would never see on screen. Walter Hill taught screenwriters that you can strip all that away. You can still direct on the page, but not by calling for specific camera movements — just by saying what you’re seeing. Walter’s scripts are made out of short sentences and white space. He looked at the placement of each line as part of the storytelling. He turned the carriage return into an art form.”.

In a recent development, as Karaszewski welcomed Hill to the stage, he pointed out that “The Getaway” — a smart, terse tale of a couple (Steve McQueen and Ali MacGraw) on the run after their involvement in a botched bank robbery — represented the emergence of Hill’s developing voice. “You’ll already see the beginnings of that remarkable style, the economy, the precision, the sense that every line is pushing you toward the next image.” Yet, as Hill revealed in his lively conversation with Karaszewski, the ruthless efficiency of the pacing and the concentrated emotional impact of “The Getaway” were not easily arrived at.

In a recent development, “I think it’s much harder to adapt than it is to write an original, which is the reverse of the normal theory,” Hill remarked. “With an original, it’s just you at your desk with the typewriter or pen. When you’re adapting, that almost always means that somebody else owns it, so you’re not simply writing based on your own opinions about what should be in and what should be out, but there’s the producer’s opinion, and the studio’s, and the actor’s. There were all these political currents that one had to navigate.”.

One such political current came from megastar McQueen, who didn’t interfere much with Hill’s writing but did have one caveat that amused the screenwriter. “He wanted to play a reasonably sympathetic outlaw,” Hill mentioned. “That was not in the Thompson sensibility. So we already had a disparity, but the producer wanted to keep Steve happy.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The Getaway” began as an assignment not for Peckinpah, but for Peter Bogdanovich, who was white-hot coming off of successes like “The Last Picture Show” and “What’s Up, Doc?” Bogdanovich didn’t last long, however, given his clashes with McQueen and McQueen’s power as the film‘s star. “I couldn’t imagine two more diverse sensibilities than Steve and Peter,” Hill mentioned, noting that he had his own disagreements with Bogdanovich over the movie’s tone but wasn’t in a position to argue. “You’ve got to remember, I was nobody. I had one screen credit. And these were significant players.”.

The massive players included not only Bogdanovich and McQueen, but MacGraw, hot off of the smash hit “Love Story.” MacGraw was pushed into the movie by her husband, Paramount studio chief Robert Evans, which Hill found amusing given the way everything played out. “I’m going to tread lightly here,” Hill said of the behind-the-scenes melodrama involving MacGraw leaving Evans when she fell in love with McQueen. “When the material was optioned and I was hired, Bob saw the movie as a fabulous idea for Steve and Ali. It didn’t work out so well for him.”.

After Bogdanovich and McQueen butted heads, Bogdanovich was let go and Peckinpah, who McQueen had enjoyed working with on “Junior Bonner,” came in to take his place. “We were very lucky to get such a talented guy, obviously,” Hill remarked. “I thought of him then and I think of him now as one of the great directors with a very unique sensibility. I was very privileged to work with him — which doesn’t mean he and I agreed about everything.”.

Sources indicate that hill’s biggest disagreement with Peckinpah had to do with a scene in which MacGraw’s character considered killing McQueen before turning the gun on his nemesis — and the man with whom MacGraw had gone to bed to secure McQueen’s early release from prison. This was a scene carried over from the book, which was darker and more paranoid than what made it to the screen given McQueen’s mandate that he be sympathetic. Hill felt that the moment no longer worked now that the relationship between McQueen and MacGraw was softer and more relatable in the novel.

“I thought that for the movie we were trying to make, you might forgive your wife for sleeping with a bad man to do a very good thing for you,” Hill stated. “That seemed to be to be conceivable. But if your wife fell into cahoots with the bad guy and actually was thinking about killing you and actually turned the gun on you before she decided to shoot the other guy…this did not track for me. But this is the screenwriter’s dilemma: you either talk the director into your point of view, or you make the change that he wants — or somebody else will. Those are your choices.”.

Hill lost the argument but liked the movie Peckinpah made in the end. “He staged it beautifully,” Hill said. “He shot it beautifully. It’s got one of Steve’s best performances. And the movie turned out to be his greatest hit. He used to call me every once in a while after I became a director and say, ‘Write me another one.'” Ironically, it was the success of “The Getaway” that put Hill in a position where didn’t have to write for other directors anymore.

In a recent development, “Larry Gordon had a producing deal to make low-budget movies at Columbia,” Hill said. “He would give young writers a chance to direct, because he said, ‘Even if they’re no good as directors, at least we’ll get a good script. Most of the directors I’m working with aren’t any good anyway.'” Gordon gave Hill the opportunity to direct “Hard Times,” and the rest was history. Aside from kicking off Hill’s directing career, the collaboration became the first of many between the two men. “He’s a wonderful guy and a wonderful producer.”.

Industry observers note that now in his 80s, Hill continues to write and direct (his last film was the exquisite character-driven Western “Dead for a Dollar“), plying his trade in the world of graphic novels in between film projects. “I’ve had four of them published in France,” Hill said, joking that the only one published in America was “the least good of them,” but promising another one on the way. “You’ve got to keep your hand in somehow.”.

As temperatures drop, our lawns often show signs of wear and tear from battling the elements. Whether dealing with patchy growth, damaged areas, or waterlogged soil, we still need to give our yards extra lawn care for the harsh winter months ahead.

Perhaps one of the most important gardening tasks for healthy lawn growth is applying fertilizer. However, given the cooler conditions, is it too late to fertilize my lawn before winter?

To answer my question, I called on the gardening experts to answer this question — and offer their top tips and tricks. So before you prep your lawn fertilizer, here’s what you need to know.

According to experts, you can fertilize your lawn before winter — as long as it’s completed by mid-November at the latest.

“If you are looking to fertilize your lawn before winter, I would recommend you do this no later than the middle of November, as your grass is becoming dormant and growth is slowing around this time, so it is best to fertilize beforehand,” advises Craig Wilson, co-founder and gardening expert at Gardeners Dream.

While fertilizing is commonly associated with warmer weather, cold-weather lawn care relies on specialized formulas.

“Make sure to use a low-nitrogen fertiliser that features high-potassium levels, as this will help to protect your lawn better in the cold weather,” adds Wilson.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months.

Furthermore, choose a fertilizer designed to specifically help your lawn withstand and handle colder weather conditions.

“Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months,” states Brian Feldman, Senior Director of Operations and Agronomy at TruGreen.

“Make sure to select a fertilizer that’s formulated specifically for fall and apply it about 3-4 weeks before your area’s first expected frost, and while soil temperatures are still above 50 degrees F.”.

Of course, prepping your lawn for winter requires a few extra steps, including clearing away weeds, clearing fallen leaves, and debris to stop them from smothering the soil underneath.

“I would also advise continuing to keep your lawn clear of fallen leaves to avoid any dead patches of grass,” agrees Wilson.

“They needn’t go to waste though — you can spread them over your borders as a nutritious mulch for your plants, which will help improve the soil quality!”.

While adding excess fertilizer seems like a good way to protect your lawn through the winter, it can actually do more harm than good. Avoid over-fertilizing if you don’t want to damage your lawn.

“Be careful not to over-fertilize, as too much can lead to nutrient runoff and weak, fast-growing grass that’s more prone to damage. The goal is strong, sustained growth from the roots up,” adds Feldman.

Other top tips include aerating your lawn and knowing when to plant grass seed in November.

Industry observers note that at this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’ Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here.

It has been revealed that the word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

Industry observers note that in both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

Sources indicate that for her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

Industry observers note that but when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

Sources indicate that de Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

According to recent reports, when Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

In a recent development, even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a newly introduced friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Calvin and Hobbes creator Bill Watterson is a genius.
  • While this selection only scratches the surface of what made Calvin and Hobbes such a brilliant creation, here are nine comic strips from the 1990s that illustrate Watterson’s incredible range as an artist.
  • One of Watterson’s recurring themes in Calvin and Hobbes was his unabashed love and admiration for the natural world, a respect he channeled right into his two leading characters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Calvin and Hobbes creator Bill Watterson is a genius. Over the course of ten years spanning more than 3,000 comic strips, he developed two truly irresistible characters that are still beloved by millions. There was a lot behind the success of Calvin and Hobbes, but I think part of the reason why Watterson is still so widely respected is that he was an incredibly versatile artist who managed to do a lot of different things in an artform that can sometimes be limiting.

While this selection only scratches the surface of what made Calvin and Hobbes such a brilliant creation, here are nine comic strips from the 1990s that illustrate Watterson’s incredible range as an artist.

One of Watterson’s recurring themes in Calvin and Hobbes was his unabashed love and admiration for the natural world, a respect he channeled right into his two leading characters. Watterson returned to this subject many times and the points he made were always thoughtful. This one, from April 1992, is especially touching, as Calvin laments that humans have lost their “awe of nature.”.

In a recent development, sometimes, Watterson seemed to use Calvin and Hobbes as an outlet for whatever major, philosophical questions were on his mind at the time. In this comic strip, Calvin and Hobbes have an in-depth conversation​​​​​​​ on the nature of luck. The best part about it is that they have it in a little wagon, careening down a giant hill. Calvin lands in some pricker bushes, which he seems to think is pretty unlucky.

Sources indicate that calvin often spoke well above the intelligence of a 6-year-old, but these comics were balanced out by adventures where Calvin is just being an imaginative little kid, like in this Sunday strip from 1995 where Calvin imagines meeting an alien who camouflages himself as Calvin. The real Calvin then goes to school pretending to be the alien, which lands him in the principal’s office.

In a recent development, in addition to mastering the joke-a-day format demanded of comic strips, sometimes Watterson would tell longer stories which spanned several days or even a couple of weeks. For example, when his arch-nemesis, Rosalyn the babysitter, came over, their encounters often became epic sagas full of twists and turns​​​​​​​, like the story from 1990 in which Calvin drove Rosalyn nuts​​​​​​​ pretending to be Stupendous Man.

Industry observers note that there were many Calvin and Hobbes strips which were incredibly heartfelt, like this tender comic from 1993 that merely shows a day in the life of Calvin and Hobbes, with both longing to be reunited​​​​​​​. The best part about it is its complete lack of dialogue.

While Watterson was capable of being thoughtful and heartfelt, some of his comic strips featured a surprisingly dark sense of humor. This side of him was best captured by the strips depicting Calvin’s snowman sculptures, which always showed snowmen going through horrific things.

According to recent reports, this strip, from Jan. 21, 1991, contains​​​​​​​ three snowman sculptures in one. The first demonstrates a snowman being shot with a cannon, the second a snowman being buried alive, and the third a snowman being hanged by a noose.​​​​​​​ That last one is especially hard to picture alongside more child-friendly newspaper comics like Peanuts and The Family Circus.

Like most other comic strips, Calvin and Hobbes had a simple drawing style, but occasionally Watterson would find an excuse to do something in much more detail, like when Calvin would pretend he was a Tyrannosaurus rex, like he does in this Halloween-themed strip from 1993.

It has been revealed that for the most part, Watterson worked within the traditional bounds of newspaper comic strips, but he never let those traditional rectangles hold him back from a really creative idea. His dinosaur comics were a great example of this, as he liked to make his dinosaurs as major as possible. Another example of Watterson breaking the traditional format is this August 1995 strip, in which Calvin had​​​​​​​ an extended internal monologue about his parents being aliens.

Of course, a collection of perfect Calvin and Hobbes comics from the 1990s would not be complete without Watterson’s final comic, which ran on Dec. 31, 1995. This open-ended sendoff was beautifully understated and deeply poignant. It could not have been better.

One of Avengers: Doomsday's heroes has been getting ready for his return off-screen.

In a recent development, shang-Chi's debut expanded the MCU by introducing audiences to Ta Lo, a hidden dimension connected to his mother's family. The mystical location played a significant role in his origin story, as he confronted his father, Wenwu, and ultimately inherited the Ten Rings. However, his first solo movie ended without fully exploring what he could do with his newly introduced powers.

With Avengers: Doomsday approaching its theatrical release, fresh details have emerged about what the superhero may have been up to during his absence. Simu Liu, who first portrayed Shang-Chi in 2021's Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, has teased how the character could have developed and improved his abilities ahead of his highly anticipated comeback.

During an interview on the Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday Official Podcast, Liu joined hosts Iman Vellani, who plays Ms. Marvel, and Frank Alvarez to discuss his character. The actor also spoke about what has transpired with the hero between his 2021 solo film and the upcoming crossover movie.

Recent findings suggest that vellani theorized that he could have spent some time at Kamar-Taj with Wong, learning more about the origins of the Ten Rings. While Liu considered that option, he came up with his own idea that would reconnect the character with his family history. According to the actor, Shang-Chi probably returned to Ta Lo after the events of his first movie. The events that occurred during his initial visit to the mystical dimension left him very little time to explore his mother's home or develop relationships with the relatives who still live there.

Liu believes that revisiting Ta Lo could provide Shang-Chi with a chance to strengthen his connection to his mother's side of the family, like his aunt Ying Nan, portrayed by Michelle Yeoh. It could also allow him to learn more about the traditions and abilities associated with the realm itself.

Industry observers note that aside from the character's personal connections, Liu explained that Shang-Chi would likely be training so he could better control the Ten Rings. Although he defeated the Dweller-in-Darkness, the actor believes his victory did not necessarily mean he had mastered everything. He further elaborated, stating that Shang-Chi's victory was the beginning of his arc. Liu explained that he would have understood the need to practice and become more comfortable with his abilities before confronting the events of Avengers: Doomsday.

Avengers: Doomsday will be released in theaters on December 18, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ChatGPT and Claude are two of the biggest names in AI, and both have become significantly more capable within the last few months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ChatGPT and Claude are two of the biggest names in AI, and both have become significantly more capable within the last few months. Whether you need help writing an email, researching a topic, creating an app or managing your workload, both chatbots can handle far more than simple questions and answers. But despite their similarities, OpenAI and Anthropic have taken different approaches to building their AI assistants.

Industry observers note that chatGPT has evolved into an all-purpose assistant with tools for everything from image generation and voice conversations to coding and research. Claude has become hyper-focused on writing, programming and helping owners complete more complicated tasks through its growing collection of productivity tools.Now that Anthropic has gone public, people are beginning to wonder what is so special about the tech giant's AI known as Claude.

I've spent plenty of time testing both, and while there's considerable overlap between what they can do, there are some differences worth understanding before deciding which one deserves your time and money.

Here are five of the biggest differences between Claude and ChatGPT.

Claude has developed a reputation for producing natural-sounding text that is especially true for longer pieces. It's also good at following detailed writing instructions and maintaining a consistent tone and style across multiple rounds of editing.

And while ChatGPT is no slouch when it comes to writing, either, it has the advantage of flexibility. You can ask it to rewrite something in five different tones, brainstorm headline ideas or transform a complicated explanation into something a beginner can understand.So, while Claude may be the better starting point for someone writing a novel or polishing a lengthy document, ChatGPT is especially useful when experimenting with different approaches.

Of course, writing quality is subjective. The results also depend on which model you're using and how clearly you explain what you want.

One of ChatGPT's biggest advantages is how many different types of tasks it can handle within the same experience.

Recent findings suggest that alongside traditional text conversations, ChatGPT supports image generation and editing. You can describe a picture you want to create, upload an existing image to change its appearance or use the chatbot to develop visual concepts.

ChatGPT also offers voice conversations, so owners can speak naturally with the assistant instead of typing everything into a chat window.

Claude has expanded its creative capabilities, too, particularly through Artifacts, which lets users create interactive content, visualizations and applications.

However, Claude's creative tools are more focused on building useful digital experiences than generating standalone images.

For anyone who regularly switches between writing, visual creation and spoken conversations, ChatGPT offers a more versatile experience.

Coding or "vibe coding" has become one of the biggest battlegrounds between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Claude Code is Anthropic's coding agent, designed to work directly with codebases, understand existing projects, make changes and help developers solve complicated programming problems.

It has become particularly popular with developers who want an AI assistant that can work inside their existing development environment.

OpenAI's answer is Codex, which can also navigate repositories, write code, fix bugs and handle development tasks.

Both tools go well beyond generating snippets of code in a chatbot. They can take on larger assignments and work through multiple steps of a project.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest difference is often how developers prefer to work. Claude Code has strong roots in terminal-based development, while Codex offers workflows across different development environments and agent-based tasks.

For casual users who occasionally need help building a website or debugging a script, either chatbot can be useful. Developers working on larger projects may find that their preferred coding agent becomes the deciding factor. Personally, I tend to hit my usage limits and blast through tokens faster with Claude Code,.

One of the most interesting changes to Claude is Anthropic's growing focus on turning the chatbot into a coworker.

According to recent reports, with Cowork, Claude can take on more complicated assignments involving files, documents and connected tools. Rather than walking through every step in a conversation, users can describe the outcome they want and let Claude work through the assignment.

For example, someone could ask Claude to organize project materials, work through a collection of documents or prepare files for a presentation.

ChatGPT is moving in a similar direction with its own agent capabilities, including ChatGPT Work and Codex.

The difference is how these experiences are organized and presented to users. Anthropic has emphasized the idea of Claude as a digital coworker that can take responsibility for larger assignments. OpenAI has built a broader ecosystem that includes conversational assistance, research, creative tools and specialized agents.

Neither approach is inherently better, but if you're looking for an AI assistant to do more than answer questions, knowing the difference is important.

Price is another consideration, particularly if you're not sure how often you'll use an AI chatbot.

Both companies offer free access, although usage limits and available features vary.

In a recent development, chatGPT Plus and Claude Pro each cost $20 per month in the United States. ChatGPT also offers a lower-priced Go subscription for $8 per month, giving people another option between the free and Plus tiers.

Claude offers annual billing for Pro, which can reduce the effective monthly cost for people willing to commit to a full year.

Industry observers note that of course, usage limits, access to more powerful models and included tools can make one subscription more valuable than another. For example, if you think you're going to be creating more images and want that type of creativity from a model, than you'll want to go with ChatGPT. At the same time, if you're a casual user looking for an affordable upgrade, ChatGPT offers more flexibility in its pricing. But, if you rely heavily on Claude's writing and coding capabilities, Pro may be worth the investment.

Here's some good news: you don't have to choose between one or the other. Because ChatGPT offers so much for free, it might be worth sticking with it. But, if you find yourself going through tokens much faster with Claude, you might want to consider bumping up your subscription to a paid tier. I use both agents for different things, which brings me to another point. The bigger question is what you want your AI assistant to do.

Claude is particularly appealing for people who spend their days writing, coding or working through complicated projects. Its emphasis on natural language and increasingly capable agent tools makes it a strong choice for serious productivity work.

ChatGPT offers a broader experience. Between image generation, voice conversations, research, coding and its growing collection of productivity features, it's designed to serve as an assistant for almost anything.

According to recent reports, if you want one AI chatbot that can handle the widest variety of everyday tasks, start with ChatGPT. If your priorities are writing, coding and managing complex workflows, Claude deserves a serious look. And since both offer free versions, the easiest way to decide is to give them the same five prompts and see which one delivers the results you actually prefer.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override.
  • If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar.
  • I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:.

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false.

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:.

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR.

Recent findings suggest that restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future enhancement.

Industry observers note that not a fan of this on macOS 27.3 beta 2. I've been a fan of “Percy Jackson” for as long as I can remember. I still remember picking up the books for the first time as a kid and getting completely swept up in Rick Riordan’s world of Greek mythology, monsters and teenage demigods. It’s a franchise I’ve had a soft spot for ever since, so seeing it find a upcoming audience through Disney’s adaptation has been a real treat. And now, somehow, we’re already heading into "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" season 3. I can’t quite believe how quickly that’s come around, but I’m certainly not complaining.

Industry observers note that season 3 adapts “The Titan's Curse,” the third book in Riordan’s beloved series. This time, Percy (Walker Scobell) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri) find themselves on a dangerous mission to rescue Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries), who has gone missing following an encounter with a mysterious latest threat. With the fate of Olympus hanging in the balance, Percy must contend with powerful enemies and a prophecy that could change everything. It’s another big adventure for the young demigods, but one that comes with considerably higher stakes.

According to recent reports, I’ve watched the first four episodes of season 3, and there’s plenty to get excited about. While the show still has the humor, friendship and sense of adventure that made me fall in love with the books in the first place, this latest chapter feels noticeably more mature. It’s an encouraging step forward for the Disney+ series, and one that makes me even more invested in seeing where these characters go next. Here’s what I thought of the first four episodes.

In a recent development, I’m Alix, a lifelong horror nerd who loves watching, reviewing and writing about the latest movies and TV reveals. When I’m not working through my ever-growing horror watchlist, I’m covering the biggest releases across streaming and film, including "VisionQuest" on Disney+, "The Institute" season 2 on MGM+, and "Guarding Stars" on Netflix.

Season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” wastes little time setting a darker, more action-packed tone. It opens with Thalia Grace (Tamara Smart) hunting for Luke (Charlie Bushnell) in a parking garage, where she finds herself battling a dangerous monster. Percy soon crashes into the fight. Thalia isn’t particularly thrilled about needing his help, which establishes some immediate friction between the two demigods. The opening also introduces the season’s central mission, with Annabeth explaining that she needs Thalia’s help to rescue two young demigods, siblings Nico (Levi Chrisopulos) and Bianca di Angelo (Olive Abercrombie).

Recent findings suggest that book readers will understand the significance of these characters straight away, while show-only viewers will get a better idea as the season unfolds. Thankfully, the first episode doesn't take long to get the main story moving, either, as Annabeth is abducted, triggering Percy’s fatal flaw: his unwavering loyalty. He’s determined to get her back, no matter how dangerous the quest becomes. That sense of danger carries through the first four episodes, and I think it’s one of the season’s biggest improvements.

Industry observers note that with the group getting older and the looming threat of war becoming increasingly difficult to ignore, the show feels noticeably more mature in its storytelling. Percy and his friends are exposed to greater dangers, and there’s a stronger sense that their actions could have serious consequences. It’s also great to see the series developing Percy’s abilities, particularly his control over water. His powers have felt somewhat underexplored in previous seasons, so watching him become more confident and capable with them is a welcome change. He’s clearly getting stronger, and I hope the remaining episodes continue to build on that.

It has been revealed that of course, you can't talk about “Percy Jackson” without mentioning Percabeth, and I know plenty of fans are just as invested in Percy and Annabeth’s developing relationship as they are in the Greek mythology. Thankfully, season 3 gives us a little more to enjoy on that front. It’s still very much a slow burn, with neither quite ready to acknowledge that their feelings might be more than friendship, but there’s a growing awareness that something special is there. The dance scene in episode 1 is a particularly lovely example of this. I suspect season 3 will give Percabeth fans plenty to get excited about.

Based on the first four episodes, season 3 is probably the strongest “Percy Jackson” season yet. I particularly appreciate is how much more attention is given to the emotional baggage these teenagers carry as the children of some incredibly powerful figures, many of whom seem largely uninterested in their own kids’ lives. including Thalia’s complicated relationship with Zeus. We get more of an insight into how these circumstances fuel their trauma and motives.

It gives the series a little more emotional depth without losing sight of the fun. The visual effects are also stronger, with the action sequences feeling grander and more cinematic than before. There’s a real sense that the show is becoming more ambitious with each season, and these early episodes have me excited to see what’s next. If the remaining episodes maintain this momentum, “Percy Jackson” could reach a whole newly introduced level, and I can only hope Disney+ has more seasons covering the rest of the books in store.

The first two episodes of "Percy Jackson" season 3 is streaming on Disney+, with the final six episodes releasing in pairs every Friday through December 11, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When iOS 27.3 beta 2 debuted earlier this week, we detailed how the revision introduces AI usage limits for Siri AI and select other features.

For AI features that depend on server-based models, each device running iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, or macOS 27.3 will have limited daily access to advanced AI features. These include complex Siri AI requests, Image Playground, certain Photos app editing tools, and more.

The only iCloud+ tier that doesn’t include higher limits is the $0.99/month plan.

Read more: Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits.

In the Shortcuts app, the ‘Use Model’ action lets you choose between a few different model options, including Cloud, Cloud Pro, On-Device, and ChatGPT.

In a recent development, people should at least have the 200 GB model. When I worked at The Apple Store (Did Retail and Corporate) I always recommended iCloud, and highlighted the backup feature. I can’t tell you the amount of people who lost or got their phones damaged / destroyed and lost precious photos, videos that they could never get back. Nearly all signed up.

Recent findings suggest that I did offer alternatives like backing to your Mac or external SSD, but to have a proper backup safety system you need 1-2 backups at home and one off site (ie. friends house, storage facility, etc.) and you would have to be consistent with your backups and drop offs. Most people don’t have the time so they do iCloud, same as I.

I’m at 2 TB, probably going to 6 TB, cause I love taking photos and videos of special events.

Similar to Apple’s other AI usage limits, your access to the Cloud Pro model in Shortcuts increases if you have a higher storage proposal. Per this support document, the 200GB plan supports standard limits, the 2TB plan offers 5x access, followed by 10x on the 6TB plan and 20x on the 12TB plan.

iCloud+ already provided far more than just increased cloud storage, but with iOS 27.3 it’s set to be an asset for AI power customers too.

iCloud+ is available as a standalone subscription or through the Apple One bundle, which also includes Apple TV, Apple Music, and more.

Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026 ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker.

It has been revealed that last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

In a recent development, winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the Newly introduced York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.
