📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

In a recent development, to aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole upcoming task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026.

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try fresh looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro mentioned the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

Recent findings suggest that “I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The vital part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro noted, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro noted. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

It has been revealed that during one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and stated, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

It has been revealed that “He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

Sources indicate that “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang noted in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the firm, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

Sources indicate that to be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

In a recent development, since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a latest CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the organization to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

What do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

#28444. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1302 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you know “the look” by now.
  • At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

In a recent development, for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

It has been revealed that those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

According to recent reports, while most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

Recent findings suggest that this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

Recent findings suggest that if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

Sources indicate that one of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In a recent development, in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

Industry observers note that the generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

Industry observers note that this is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

In a recent development, to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

Steven Spielberg’s 13-Part Sci-Fi Series Is So Good, You’ll Finish It in One Weekend

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few things are as creepy as children in horror films and TV series.
  • The Whispers opens with a playful scene, as children in a yard run through sprinklers, blow bubbles, and do what kids do.
  • It has been revealed that what the game is, no one knows, but it involves Harper collecting tools and going up into the treehouse, where she's not supposed to be alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few things are as creepy as children in horror films and TV series. What's scarier? Children who are being manipulated by something — or someone — unknown, that is. It's doubtful that The Exorcist would have been as effective had Regan (Linda Blair) been an adult, or Sinister as seriously messed up as it is if Bughuul did his dirty work through senior citizens. This brings us to The Whispers, a forgotten, 13-part sci-fi horror series that premiered on ABC in 2015 from executive producer Steven Spielberg, where children communicate with an entity known only as Drill, who promises them rewards if they play his "games," resulting in a series of incidents that seemingly have no connection… until they do. Eleven years later, its creepy premise still makes an ordinary childhood friendship feel like a threat.

The Whispers opens with a playful scene, as children in a yard run through sprinklers, blow bubbles, and do what kids do. That is, except Harper (Abby Ryder Fortson), who's off to the side, talking to someone we can only assume is an imaginary friend she's named Drill. Her mother, Amanda (Autumn Reeser), calls her in, much to Harper's chagrin. She hasn't learned all the rules for the game Drill wants her to play yet.

It has been revealed that what the game is, no one knows, but it involves Harper collecting tools and going up into the treehouse, where she's not supposed to be alone. Amanda storms out, but Harper won't come down, claiming that it's part of the game, and Drill says that Amanda is now "it." Amanda climbs up, walks to an "X" drawn on the floor, and promptly crashes through, hitting the ground, seriously injuring her and sending her into a coma.

According to recent reports, it's the opening salvo in a battle against an unknown entity, one that may be supernatural or even alien in nature, and one that picks and chooses the children it "whispers" to further its own agenda. It's up to Special Agent Claire Bennigan (Lily Rabe), an FBI child specialist, and Wes Lawrence (Barry Sloane), a high-ranking Defense Department operative, to find out who or what Drill is, why he's targeting children for his games, and what his endgame could be.

In a recent development, it takes on an increased urgency for each of them, given they all have their own children. Additionally, Claire's husband, U.S. Air Force pilot Captain Sean Bennigan (Milo Ventimiglia), who was thought to have died in a plane crash, is part of Drill's game. And Drill's always one step ahead.

It has been revealed that the Whispers seamlessly blends sci-fi and horror with an unsettling eeriness, deepening and building the mystery with an underlying, ever-increasing anxiety. (And yes, it's thanks to those creepy kids.) Each of the young actors in primary roles — Fortson, Kyle Harrison Breitkopf, Kylie Rogers, and Kayden Magnuson — is brilliant, playing innocents unaware (maybe) of the consequences of playing Drill's games (Magnuson is particularly chilling in the finale). The adult cast, too, is strong. Ventimiglia is the strongest of the adult cast, playing what is essentially two different characters in the first and second half of the season.

The Whispers also bears an undeniable mark of its executive producer: the exploration of the adult/child dynamic. The children listen to Drill and are willing to do his bidding because he listens to them, and the adults in their lives don't. From Hook to The Fabelmans to E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial, there's a repeated theme of the disconnect between adults and children in Spielberg's works. Adults are absent, oblivious, and even antagonistic, and that's no different in The Whispers. The children are told that they're not allowed to talk to their imaginary friend. They leave their homes — despite so-called adult supervision — to carry out Drill's instructions in perilous ways.

While most Spielberg fare has adults learning to pay more attention to their children, The Whispers ends on a life lesson, faced with the consequences of adults not paying attention until it's too late. It begs the question: who is the real danger, Drill or the parents? It's actually Drill who makes the argument for the latter, saying: "If parents paid more attention to them, I wouldn't have been able to [corrupt them]. But they're always alone, watching TV, playing video games. So, who's really corrupting the children, Claire?".

Recent findings suggest that but it's a question that would go unanswered, along with a host of others, with ABC pulling the plug on The Whispers after one season that ends on a major, unresolved cliffhanger. Don't let that stop you: The Whispers is the perfect weekend binge that keeps the viewer engaged from start to finish, and is a thrilling and eerie ride worth taking. Unless your child starts talking to an imaginary friend.

The Whispers is available to buy digitally on Amazon in the U.S.; a Prime subscription does not include it.

Sources indicate that marvel’s ventures have been very successful in 2026, but it is now officially the end of an era for the TV side of the franchise. Upcoming Marvel movies will move the MCU back into more mainstream territory, with two Avengers films, an X-Men story, and Black Panther 3 hitting theaters in the next few years. This comes after a period in which Marvel Studios has arguably put more focus into crafting small-screen stories set in the MCU on Disney+.

In a recent development, despite a somewhat mixed bag of projects releasing between 2021 and 2025, Marvel’s 2026 TV highlights have been excellent. Be it Daredevil: Born Again season 2, VisionQuest, and the brilliantly unique Wonder Man in live-action or animated ventures like X-Men ‘97, Marvel Television seems to be hitting its stride of late. However, in a cruel situation involving unfortunate timing, Marvel’s TV era is seemingly at an end.

2026’s VisionQuest was a huge success in many ways; from a self-contained story about humanity and grief to a sequel to WandaVision and a stepping stone to Avengers: Doomsday, VisionQuest worked on all fronts. That said, where the former and latter points are concerned, VisionQuest does seem like the end of Marvel’s TV dominance. The show is the final one before the release of Avengers: Doomsday, and the second-to-last live-action show confirmed to be released before Avengers: Secret Wars in December 2027.

It has been revealed that what this means is that, besides Daredevil: Born Again season 3, which is as self-contained as MCU shows can get, VisionQuest ends the Disney+ era of the franchise before upcoming movies change everything. Avengers: Doomsday will begin the end of the Multiverse Saga and, with no projects but Daredevil: Born Again season 3 set for release in the main MCU universe between it and Avengers: Secret Wars, it will likely change the multiverse drastically. Adding in the soft reboot of Avengers: Secret Wars, which will change Marvel TV forever, VisionQuest is truly the end of an era.

VisionQuest ending the current MCU TV era only makes the future of the franchise on the small screen more unclear than ever. As alluded to, Daredevil: Born Again season 3 will release in 2027, though the show has been canceled beyond that, meaning it will likely end that section of the franchise. After 2027, only one MCU TV show remains in development: Zodiac. As of right now, it is unclear what Zodiac is, what it is about, or who will be part of the series. Moreover, it is set for release after Avengers: Secret Wars' reboot of the MCU.

Other than that, Marvel Television has only standalone animated TV projects to produce, from Marvel Zombies to Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man, which exist within their own continuities. All this reinforces how VisionQuest is the true end of an era for Marvel Television, as the future will only house standalone projects and those due to end soon, while the movie side of the franchise resets everything in massive ways.

In a recent development, although the lack of clarity surrounding Marvel TV's future is worrying, VisionQuest concluded its most recent era in the best way possible. For one, on a broader level, VisionQuest was simply one of the studio's best Disney+ reveals. Marvel TV has had as many hits as misses since 2021. The fact that the studio ended on such a high certainly makes things sweeter for Marvel and its audiences alike. Moreover, VisionQuest was a deeper, thematic conclusion for the WandaVision trilogy, which began in 2021 and has permeated Marvel TV since.

Not only was VisionQuest a good ending, quality-wise, but it signified the end of the Marvel TV storyline that started it all on Disney+ in 2021. Finally, VisionQuest's post-credit scene is one of the most exciting the MCU has produced in years, teasing Doctor Doom's upcoming rampage and the resurrection of the Scarlet Witch. This was the best way to signify the MCU's transition into the Avengers-fueled era that is about to ensue over the next year or so, only further solidifying VisionQuest as a fitting, exciting, thematically fruitful end of an era for Marvel Television.

  • Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in Fresh York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

The original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

In a recent development, the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6 maintains the fast, versatile ride the line is known for while adding a little more comfort, making it a successful if minor upgrade on the Endorphin Speed 5. It’s one of the best fast trainers available and if you’ve loved past models, the Speed 6 is unlikely to disappoint, but there are some fantastic alternatives to consider too.

Stable and comfortable at easy paces.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Saucony Endorphin Speed has been one of the most influential running shoes of recent years, setting the template for fast training sneakers that uses some of the materials and tech from top carbon plate racers.

With the line proving so successful, Saucony has been reluctant to change much about the shoe over the five generations to date, and even though the Endorphin Speed 6 is the biggest patch yet thanks to a newly introduced midsole foam, it mostly retains the same ride feel as past models.

Sources indicate that I’ve reviewed every model of the Endorphin Speed and I’ve always been a substantial fan. While that’s still true with the Speed 6, this category contains some of the best running shoes available, and there are some lighter, bouncier fast trainers I rate very highly, like the Upcoming Balance SC Rebel v1 and Dynafish Xiaonian.

In a recent development, the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6 costs $180 in the U.S. and £180 in the U.K., which is a $5 price rise on the Endorphin Speed 5. It’s an expensive shoe, though not out of line with other plated trainers like the Hoka Mach X3 and Upcoming Balance SC Rebel v1.

Right now the Saucony Endorphin Speed 5 is widely reduced, dropping to $104 on Amazon in the Black Friday sales, which is a factor to consider when weighing up buying the Speed.

The Endorphin Speed 6 is currently available in five colors in the women’s shoe, and four colors in the men’s, including the white and yellow design I tested.

There is a wide version of the shoe available, though I found that the standard one fit me well in my normal running shoe size, the same size I’ve used with all past models of the shoe.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Saucony has added 2mm of foam to the midsole of the Endorphin Speed 6, which has a stack height of 38mm at the heel and 30mm at the forefoot, maintaining the 8mm drop of past models.

It weighs in at 8.5oz, which is 0.5oz lighter than the Endorphin Speed 5 in my size, a welcome drop for a speed-focused shoe.

The Endorphin Speed 6 has a simple mesh upper that has a little bit of padding around the tongue and collar, but mostly focuses on being lightweight and breathable.

It’s my preferred kind of upper on any shoe, since it’s not oppressively padded on the tongue or overly stiff around the heel, and I found the fit comfortable and secure throughout all my runs.

The Endorphin Speed 6’s main changes are in the midsole, which is made from a latest foam called PWRRUN PBX, which is meant to be lighter and bouncier than the PWRRUN PB that has been used on all past models of the shoe.

There’s also the higher stack and a redesigned nylon plate in the midsole, which aims to create a smoother, faster ride, with the Speedroll rocker on the shoe also contributing to this.

The changes to the midsole are noticeable on the run, though not as dramatically as I expected when looking at the spec sheet for the Speed 6.

Rubber is used sparingly on the bottom of the Speed 6 to keep the weight down, but patches cover the forefoot and heel of the shoe, and in my experience Saucony’s pelletized midsole foams are durable even when the foam is exposed on the bottom of a shoe.

Grip hasn’t always been a positive feature on the Speed line, but the Speed 6 provided me with reliable traction in wet conditions on both the road and the track during my testing.

After the very pleasant surprise of the original Endorphin Speed, which I ran over 300 miles in, I’ve found that the line has delivered a reliably similar experience with all of the models since.

There have been updates to make it more stable and comfortable, but ultimately all five versions of the Speed to date have had a smooth, fast and versatile ride feel.

This is still true of the Endorphin Speed 6 for me, and while that’s mostly a positive in that it performed well across a variety of runs in my testing, some might have hoped for a bigger change to challenge rivals like the SC Rebel v1 and cheaper, lighter options like the Adidas Adizero Evo SL and Dynafish Xiaonian.

I used the shoe for a couple of easy runs, two progression runs moving from easy to tempo pace, and a threshold track workout running 4 x 8min reps, and it felt great throughout.

I used the shoe for a couple of easy runs, two progression runs moving from easy to tempo pace, and a threshold track workout running 4 x 8min reps, and it felt great throughout.

The rockered midsole pushes you smoothly through your footstrike, and while the midsole foam isn’t as soft and springy as some, it does give a good amount of energy return off the toes.

I also found the Speed 6 to be quite stable and comfortable for easy runs, which is not always the case with plated trainers like this. I could happily use it for pretty much any kind of run, though it’s not as fast as a true carbon plate racer, or as comfortable as a max-cushioned cruiser.

To compare it directly to the Endorphin Speed 5 I did a short run wearing both shoes, and while the Speed 6 is a little bouncier and more comfortable, especially under the forefoot, I still felt the two shoes had a similar ride feel.

The Speed 6 is still a bit firmer than most super-trainers, and not as comfortable as more cushioned shoes under the toes. Some will like this more direct ride feel, but I appreciate the extra softness and bounce of a shoe like the SC Rebel v1.

Industry observers note that if you’re a long term fan of the Endorphin Speed line the Speed 6 will be a winner. It’s a mild improvement on the previous models with extra cushion and bounce, and delivers the versatile performance you expect from the line.

There is certainly a case for getting the Speed 5 instead in sales in my opinion, but the Speed 6 is a slightly better shoe overall and a successful update.

The Speed line has been faced with increasingly fierce competition in recent years, and I don’t think the Speed 6 does much to change the equation on this front.

If you want a lighter, bouncier fast trainer, the New Balance SC Rebel v1 would be my pick, while plate-free shoes like the Adidas Evo SL, Dyanfish Xiaonian and the new 361° Mega 3 Pro all offer fast, fun rides at a lower price.

As someone who would always have had the Endorphin Speed in my own rotation through the first few models, I’ve now moved on to shoes like this myself. Even though the Speed 6 is just as good as past models, I personally like the springier ride available in fast trainers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside upcoming features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a newly introduced alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the manufacturer’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the tech giant’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing people to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:.

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

In a recent development, the first thing consumers will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

Recent findings suggest that as for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the manufacturer’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for rapidly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

It has been revealed that and speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for people looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are latest organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow people to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Recent findings suggest that once owners are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, consumers can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

According to recent reports, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:.

How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • According to recent reports, “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

According to recent reports, “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

It has been revealed that “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

Sources indicate that for Crawford, the substantial lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

Industry observers note that “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

Recent findings suggest that still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado noted. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

Industry observers note that this all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford stated, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

10 Greatest Netflix Demonstrates With Fewer Than 30 Episodes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, netflix has frequently proven that good things come in small packages when it comes to original television shows.
  • Netflix has released hundreds of indicates over the years, and many were axed after the first season for reasons ranging from budget to low viewership.
  • Once Netflix owners watch five minutes of Blue Eye Samurai, they will wish they'd watched this show sooner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, netflix has frequently proven that good things come in small packages when it comes to original television shows. Some of them had short episode counts on purpose, while others were canceled too soon. The number of episodes doesn't define a television show's quality, but it can play a role in how impactful the series is for audiences.

Netflix has released hundreds of indicates over the years, and many were axed after the first season for reasons ranging from budget to low viewership. However, the streaming platform has a pattern of releasing critically acclaimed miniseries, and low-episode-count shows have been turning into cult classics. With that in mind, here is our list of the greatest Netflix shows with fewer than 30 episodes that are available to stream right now.

Once Netflix owners watch five minutes of Blue Eye Samurai, they will wish they'd watched this show sooner. The show follows Mizu (Maya Erskine), a mixed-race Japanese warrior who is seeking vengeance against the men who may be responsible for her birth. She does all this disguised as a boy, and adjusts to being accompanied by Ringo (Masi Oka), and later teaming up with Taigen (Darren Barnet).

What makes one of the greatest samurai TV indicates refreshing is the decision to redefine gender stereotypes, even though the characters don't know this is happening. Mizu's personal story is painful to take in, but it's her history that gives her the strength to fight and destroy the opponents who underestimate her. All the voice actors were phenomenal at turning up the hype, which will grow following the Season 2 premiere, and continue to build in the months leading up to the third and final season.

Although this show lasted only two seasons, Russian Doll has aged like fine wine thanks to the heart and unique humor put into it. The series follows Nadia Vulvokov (Natasha Lyonne), a software engineer who keeps dying and reliving her 36th birthday party in an ongoing time loop. The belief that she is hallucinating in a nightmare takes a shocking turn when she meets Alan Zaveri (Charlie Barnett), who, like her, is living in a time loop, and dying all the time.

Industry observers note that lyonne, who is one of the show's co-creators, is known for applying humor so naturally to any character she portrays, even in serious films or television indicates. Her performance in Russian Doll was no different; and the combination of her personality with Nadia's made viewers see the connection the actress shares with Nadia, while watching her character learn about life and undergoing personal growth. Although Russian Doll may have become a show audiences have never heard of, they won't forget it once they watch one of its 15 episodes on Netflix.

According to recent reports, derry Girls was already one of the best dark comedy TV shows of all time, and aired on Channel 4 in the United Kingdom before it became available to stream internationally on Netflix. The show focuses on the lives of Erin Quinn (Saoirse-Monica Jackson), Orla McCool (Louisa Harland), Claire Devlin (Nicola Coughlan), Michelle Mallon (Jamie-Lee O'Donnell), and James Maguire (Dylan Llewellyn), in the 1990s during Ireland's political conflict, The Troubles. The teenagers go through typical, coming-of-age situations in school and with their parents, but as time goes on, they begin to pay closer attention to the political situation around them.

It may be hard to imagine that a dark comedy is also one of the most educational representations of The Troubles in the eyes of adolescents and adults. Every actor portrayed reality with grace, and it was phenomenal to see the show's plots backed up by archive footage of things like news stories, and a speech delivered by then-President Bill Clinton in Derry back in 1995. Although Derry Girls had enough popularity to last for years, series creator Lisa McGee always planned to end the show after Season 3, which makes it one of the best TV shows under 20 episodes.

This 10-episode miniseries is not only the greatest horror miniseries of all time, but it's also one that audiences may not want to watch alone in the dark. The Haunting of Hill House demonstrates the terrifying story of the Crain family, and their experience living and eventually fleeing a haunted mansion in 1992, without the family matriarch. Years later, Stephen Crain (Michiel Huisman), Shirley Crain Harris (Elizabeth Reaser), Luke Crain (Oliver Jackson-Cohen), and Theodora "Theo" Crain (Kate Siegel) are estranged, but reunited following an increase of strange occurrences, including visions of their late sister, Eleanor "Nell" Crain Vance (Victoria Pedretti).

Recent findings suggest that every young and adult actor's performance is undeniably amazing, and their commitment to highlighting their characters’ trauma and coping mechanisms only makes the horror more real for viewers. Although the characters' experiences made this one of the scariest TV shows of all time, it also made viewers have a new appreciation for family members, especially their parents and siblings. Pedretti and Jackson-Cohen are among the multiple actors who returned to play different characters in the follow-up miniseries, The Haunting of Bly Manor, which is also considered one of the best horror miniseries.

In a recent development, baby Reindeer is full of mind-blowing plot twists that fans love to keep up with. The show begins with Donny Dunn (Richard Gadd) attempting to file a police report after claiming he was being stalked by Martha Scott (Jessica Gunning), a lawyer who is no stranger to criminal mischief. Their encounters go from harmless to chilling, and her harassment worsens to the point where Donny is no longer the only victim in her latest round of stalking behavior. Although Martha's actions are hair-raising, they were needed for Donny to begin facing his fears, and accept who he is.

Sources indicate that gadd and Gunning's chemistry was undeniable in the most creepy way possible. The actors' passion in their performances proved to viewers that they were the only stars who could play these roles, and it was easy to feel Martha's anger and Donny's intimidation just by looking at their faces in all seven episodes. Their performances were only part of the reason why this show is one of the best miniseries of the 2020s, and they each took home a Golden Globe Award to prove it.

Mindhunter will always be a canceled crime show worth watching that deserves more than two seasons. Based on the true-crime book Mindhunter: Inside the FBI's Elite Serial Crime Unit, the show revolves around FBI agents, Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany), who, along with Wendy Carr (Anna Torv), interview and seek information from serial killers about their crimes and motivations, and apply that information to future cases. Set in the '70s and early '80s, viewers get an inside look into the early years of the Behavioral Science Unit, which is known for helping law enforcement with brutal crimes, and preventing terrorism.

Industry observers note that groff did not waste any time creating the personality of a no-nonsense agent seeking ways to improve the FBI. It was a 180 from his Glee character, Jesse St. James, and it showed viewers that Groff can go outside his comfort zone. The show could've had the potential to become an Emmy and Golden Globe Award winner if it hadn't been canceled, but it will always be one of the darkest TV dramas of the last 10 years.

Beth Harmon (Anya Taylor-Joy) portrays a chess player out for blood in this seven-episode miniseries. The Queen's Gambit explores Beth's journey to reach her dream of becoming a grandmaster, all while battling addiction and overcoming family drama in her birth and adoptive families. Her journey takes her all over the world with her adoptive mother, Alma Wheatley (Marielle Heller), and helps her form bonds with multiple chess players, including D.L. Townes (Jacob Fortune-Loyd), Harry Beltik (Harry Melling), and Benny Watts (Thomas Brodie-Sangster).

Taylor-Joy found the right balance between determination and intensity in her performance, and made it clear to viewers that she was the only person who could accurately portray the perfection-seeking Beth. Her character only wanted perfection, and when that didn't happen, a glimpse of the depression she hid from the world surfaced. Taylor-Joy showed audiences that even a perfect person is haunted by something, and her Golden Globe-winning performance helped make The Queen's Gambit one of the greatest Netflix miniseries of all time.

This German-language show is raw, complex, and one of the best sci-fi mystery indicates of all time. Dark is set in Winden, a small town startled by the disappearance of two children, leaving families to suffer the collateral damage that comes of it. Jonas Kahnwad (Louis Hofmann), a teenager reeling over the loss of his father, soon discovers the disappearances, and other town secrets, are connected to a time-travel loop.

Unlike some sci-fi series, Dark puts characters front and center, and factors in their emotions when exploring the time traveling and supernatural aspects of the show. Audiences may still be surprised to learn it's one of the best Netflix shows with three seasons, especially since the complexity seems too much to fit into only 26 episodes. Everything came together by the end of the series, and while some viewers may now be afraid to start families, they were able to witness a satisfying ending that concluded all character arcs.

When They See Us is not only one of the saddest miniseries of all time, it's also based on the true story of the 1989 Central Park jogger case. The first two episodes center around the arrests of Kevin Richardson (Asante Blackk), Antron McCray (Caleel Harris), Yusef Salaam (Ethan Herisse), Raymond Santana (Marquis Rodriguez), and Korey Wise (Jharrel Jerome), for the assault and rape of Trisha Meili (Alexandra Templer), and the events leading up to their confessions and convictions. The final two episodes show the difficulty of some of these men returning to society, Wise's treatment in prison, and the truth behind what happened to Trisha in Central Park.

Industry observers note that every actor's facial expressions throughout the miniseries represented the pain the Exonerated Five and their families felt during the events leading up to their exoneration. However, Jerome's outstanding performance shook audiences to their core, and the Emmy Award-winning actor portrayed the fear Korey may have had in prison beautifully. The Central Park jogger case has become an example of racial profiling and discrimination in the media and legal system, and When They See Us provides viewers with a detailed explanation as to why.

Sources indicate that adolescence is a miniseries that's a 10/10 masterpiece that is both brilliant and terrifying. The four-episode show centers around Jamie Miller (Owen Cooper), a 13-year-old boy accused of brutally murdering a classmate. His arrest leads to shocking details about the events before and after the crime, as well as the pain his family endures from everyone who is furious at Jamie.

In a recent development, miller's performance was unforgettably brilliant, and it's still hard to believe that this was his debut acting role, even a year after the miniseries premiered. It's usually difficult for an adult actor to give audiences chills for their antagonistic performance on a television show, but Miller had no problem doing so during the third and best Adolescence episode. Besides Miller, Stephen Graham and Erin Doherty were phenomenal in portraying the vulnerability and emotions behind each character, and their performances led to the trio each winning an Emmy and a Golden Globe Award.

Industry News: Curry Barker Would Have Completely Reshot ‘Obsession’ If He Could

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-announced third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a Latest Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

According to recent reports, “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really quickly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” noted Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

It has been revealed that “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

“People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” remarked Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how quickly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

In a recent development, directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

It has been revealed that what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, rapidly claims he fell short in “Obsession.”.

Industry observers note that “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” stated Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” noted Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

Recent findings suggest that as Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

  • In a recent development, you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers.
  • It has been revealed that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

In a recent development, you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

It has been revealed that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

Recent findings suggest that in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

Industry observers note that as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber reveals up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!
