How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • Industry observers note that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Industry observers note that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he stated through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation A ‘Home Alone’ Legacyquel with Macaulay Culkin in Early Development with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg.

It has been revealed that but he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I remarked, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

In a recent development, at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he mentioned. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

Industry observers note that his 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

Recent findings suggest that how’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

Recent findings suggest that the filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

Industry observers note that when it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he noted. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Recent findings suggest that of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he remarked. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

Recent findings suggest that the filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he mentioned. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Industry observers note that was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he mentioned, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

Or even just a 60fps enhancement. Anything. However, with Sony seemingly dragging its feet despite FromSoftware itself being on board with the project, it may be another decade until we see Bloodborne make its grand return.

That being remarked, there is still plenty to look forward to if you want to immerse yourself in the Bloodborne universe, and in May 2027, the FromSoftware magnum opus returns with a stunning newly introduced collection.

Recent findings suggest that courtesy of Good Smile Organization, pre-orders for a re-release of its Hunter Figma are now open and showcases our protagonist as they appear in Bloodborne's The Old Hunters DLC. Complete with the iconic hat and garb, the figure is also capable of being transformed into different poses thanks to adjustable joints, and not only that, but the upcoming release also comes with multiple weapons from both the base game and DLC which can be attached depending on your chosen pose. Last but not least, the Hunter Figma statue comes alongside a stand to help display your collectible even easier.

Recent findings suggest that set to release in May 2027, Hunter Figma showcases the iconic Saw Cleaver, Hunter Pistol, Hunter Blunderbuss, Hunter Axe, Whirligig Saw, and Ludwig's Holy Blade, and fans will be pleased to learn that the Saw Cleaver can even be extended. So how much will all of this cost? The upcoming re-release retails at ￥12,800, which is the equivalent of 80.30 USD, so, as figures go, it is a pretty respectable price for Bloodborne collectors. The full list of features include:.

・Using the smooth yet posable joints of figma, you can create a variety of poses.

・A flexible plastic is used for key areas, allowing proportions to be kept without compromising posability.

・Both the Saw Cleaver and Hunter Pistol are included as weapons for the Hunter to wield.

・The Saw Cleaver can be transformed into its extended cleaver form just like in the game.

・The Old Hunters Edition also includes the Hunter Blunderbuss, the Hunter Axe, the Whirligig Saw and Ludwig's Holy Blade.

・The Hunter Axe, Whirligig Saw and Ludwig's Holy Blade come with interchangeable parts to display them in their transformed forms.

・Special attachment parts are included to display the Whirligig Saw and Ludwig's Holy Blade on the back of the Hunter.

・Hand parts to display the Hunter holding each weapon are included.

・An articulated figma stand is included to display the figma in a variety of poses.

Recent findings suggest that limited to three figures per person, this re-release from Good Smile Manufacturer is not one that Bloodborne fans will want to miss out on again, and whilst it may not be the Bloodborne PC port or remaster we have all been waiting for, it is definitely the next best thing. With the protagonist sporting one of the most iconic looks in gaming history, you can now commemorate it on your display case for good, and for quite a reasonable price.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Mummy movies are a celebrated blend of action, adventure, and comedy that still remain popular — and immensely quotable —decades after the first film’s 1999 release. There are many memorable lines that fans of the trilogy will quote to each other, from the swashbuckling Rick O’Connell (Brendan Fraser) declaring: “I only gamble with my life, never my money,” or Dr. Bey (Erick Avari) despairing: “When Rameses destroyed Syria, that was an accident. You are a catastrophe!” However, one quote from the original movie stands out as the greatest in the whole series. Spoken by Evelyn Carnahan (Rachel Weisz), it defines exactly why, with the fourth movie on the horizon, we hold the world of these films so close to our hearts.

Industry observers note that for the uninitiated, 1999’s The Mummy follows Evelyn, a librarian and aspiring Egyptologist who, along with her brother Jonathan (John Hannah), free adventurer Rick O’Connell from prison so that he can help them find a mythical location, where they accidentally awaken the cursed high priest Imhotep. Along with a series of delightful action sequences, the film focuses on the clash of personalities between bookworm Evelyn and cavalier treasure hunter Rick.

It’s this difference in worldviews that leads to the film’s best line. In a drunken moment beside a campfire, Evelyn declares: “I may not be an explorer, or an adventurer, or a treasure-seeker, or a gunfighter, Mr. O’Connell, but I am proud of what I am.” Amused, Rick asks: “And what is that?”, before Evelyn looks to the middle distance, smiles, and replies: “I... am a librarian.” It’s a moment of comedy, but one that also sums up the charming relationship at the center of this film and the 2001 sequel, The Mummy Returns. Weisz was unavailable for the 2008 third movie, The Mummy: The Tomb of the Dragon Emperor, replaced by Maria Bello, but her return for the fourth film, right now in production, was celebrated by fans precisely because of the dynamic that this speech encapsulates.

In a recent development, the Mummy movies have broadly the same appeal as the Indiana Jones franchise, with exotic locations, ancient mysteries, and colorful characters populating a rich and entertaining world. While they may attract similar audiences, The Mummy differentiated itself from the classic Steven Spielberg franchise by making two characters the focus, rather than a single adventurer with a secondary character who serves as a potential love interest. The Mummy doesn’t work without Evelyn and Rick bantering, as well as using their very different skills in order to achieve their goals. Evelyn’s speech, while funny, highlights how crucial that dynamic is to the story.

It has been revealed that rick is strong, courageous, and charismatic, getting the group out of more than one dangerous moment over the course of the movies. However, it takes more than his heroism to get the job done. Evelyn’s brains, instincts, and curiosity are vital to their discovering hidden wonders, making her as notable to the movie as her future husband. She is not a sidekick, or a damsel in distress, but an equal partner in an on-screen coupling that made Hollywood magic. There’s no Rick without Evelyn, giving her every right to cherish her love of knowledge.

The fourth movie in the franchise, The Mummy: Book of the Dead, is right now filming for a planned 2027 release. The first images of Weisz in costume as Evelyn recently emerged online, with fans delighted to see her stylish return to the beloved role. The popularity of the leak stems from fans who grew up with the movies acknowledging her as a vital part of the franchise, someone that audiences are keen to see as an older woman, a mother, still tearing across the world in search of adventure.

It has been revealed that many movies have had long-awaited sequels in recent years – Gladiator and Beetlejuice both got follow-ups in 2024, while fellow globe-trotter Indiana Jones came back for one last mission in 2023’s The Dial of Destiny. By the time the fourth Mummy film arrives, it will have been 17 years since the last time we saw an entry in the saga, and 26 since we saw Weisz play Evelyn. So why are fans so excited to see her back? Because, in all that time, her wit and fearlessness have been replayed on home video and streaming services for an entire generation. She is a character that endured because of her nerdiness, not in spite of it. We love this librarian and celebrate her return.

The Mummy has been adapted twice since this action-adventure trilogy was released: in 2017 as a Tom Cruise blockbuster, and in 2026 with Lee Cronin’s The Mummy. Both were poorly received, both critically and by theater audiences, and perhaps the reason for that is the affection with which Evelyn and Rick are held in the hearts of movie fans. Maybe you don’t need elevated scares or plane crash sequences to make a hit. Perhaps you just need a librarian.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a newly introduced popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’ How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation.

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

Recent findings suggest that but while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he mentioned. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump stated his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump stated. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

It has been revealed that trump mentioned Georgia and Fresh Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Industry observers note that trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors declared more than 60 upcoming House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he mentioned, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

Industry observers note that “Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she said in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

A floor vote has yet to be revealed, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff mentioned.

Tech Report: Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • Industry observers note that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • It has been revealed that perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

Industry observers note that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

It has been revealed that perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

Sources indicate that I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an problem with the Duo itself.

It has been revealed that I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

According to recent reports, multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Sources indicate that last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

Industry observers note that I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

In a recent development, I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

Sources indicate that I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Recent findings suggest that is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

In a recent development, the iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique newly introduced iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

In a recent development, what has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

Breaking: I tested the Hyundai Ioniq 9 again for the second time this year — don't let its polarizing design fool you

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quite frankly, the Hyundai Ioniq 9 gets a bad rap for the way it looks.
  • That’s why I drove the Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design for the second time this year — just to convince myself that there are better 3-row midsize SUVs out there.
  • But after another week behind the wheel, I can tell you firsthand that judging the Ioniq 9 by its cover is a mistake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quite frankly, the Hyundai Ioniq 9 gets a bad rap for the way it looks. In fact, I said in my 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 review that the design is an “odd mashup featuring a curvy front bumper with an even stranger-looking arched rear.” It’s one of the last SUVs I’d expect to win any beauty awards.

That’s why I drove the Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design for the second time this year — just to convince myself that there are better 3-row midsize SUVs out there. I’ve spent more time testing 3-row SUVs than any other vehicle type this year, with models like the Kia Telluride, Volvo XC90, Volkswagen Atlas, and Lucid Gravity getting my seal of approval.

But after another week behind the wheel, I can tell you firsthand that judging the Ioniq 9 by its cover is a mistake. Here’s what I realized.

Best long distance driving efficiency.

Best short distance driving efficiency.

As with most vehicles, fuel economy and efficiency tend to dwindle over time — which is why I’m shocked that the Ioniq 9 is an exception. I was already impressed by the 3 mi/kWh average I got when I drove it last year, yet my second run delivered even better results.

Sources indicate that across 130.5 miles of mixed driving, my second go-around with the Ioniq 9 yielded an impressive 3.3 mi/kWh. What surprised me even more was the substantial improvement in city driving, where I recorded a peak tally of 4.5 mi/kWh — up from my previous best of 3.8 mi/kWh.

In a recent development, considering it’s marketed as a three-row family hauler, it’s remarkable that the Ioniq 9 can post numbers like this. That extra efficiency is critical, too: while this trim carries an EPA-estimated range of 311 miles, averaging 3.3 mi/kWh puts its real-world range closer to 363 miles.

I’ll admit I was harsh on the Hyundai Ioniq 9’s styling the first time around. While it certainly takes cues from the subcompact Hyundai Kona, I argued that it was an odd mashup that was confused about what aesthetic it was trying to go after.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It has been revealed that after spending another week with it, though, its unconventional look slowly grew on me — even if that appreciation is mostly isolated to the front of the EV. That’s due to Hyundai’s signature Parametric Pixel LED light bar, which stretches across the nose like something straight out of a sci-fi movie. Those individual blocks give it a retro look that becomes even more dazzling from dusk into the night. In a sea of generic crossovers, this one certainly commands road presence.

That mentioned, I still haven’t come to terms with the back half of this electric SUV. That tapered, upright rear end remains the hardest pill to swallow, giving it the look of a boat tail. Despite this, I now appreciate that the shape is doing the heavy lifting to make it aerodynamic — and subsequently boosting its efficiency.

According to recent reports, whether I’m making a quick stop at the local grocery store or on my 30+ mile commute to work, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 doesn’t skimp on the comforts. Step inside, and it’s clear Hyundai prioritized first-class comfort for the people riding up front and in the middle.

According to recent reports, for example, the plush H-Tex seats strike a great balance of softness and support — which, for the driver, includes extra pampering courtesy of Hyundai’s Ergo Motion seat. When activated, it slowly adjusts the firmness of the cushion, sort of like getting a mini massage while driving, all to deter fatigue on longer hauls.

Sources indicate that still, the real VIP treatment belongs to the second-row captain’s chairs. With both heating and ventilation, plus power-reclining backrests and extendable footrests, they turn the middle row into a rolling lounge. However, the third row leaves more to be desired. Although I still appreciate having the extra seating capacity in a pinch, the legroom back there is practically nonexistent for adults — so I’d much rather keep that rear bench folded flat to make way for more trunk space.

At nearly $80,000 as tested, the Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design comes loaded with just about every luxury and tech perk anyone could ask for — and rightfully so.

​I still absolutely love Hyundai's adaptive cruise control, which makes long drives bearable and includes a dedicated lane-centering button on the steering wheel that also happens to work on local roads. Adding to that is a crisp Head-Up Display that projects my speed and navigation right onto the windshield.

​Changing lanes is effortless thanks to the Blind-Spot View Monitor (which streams a live camera feed straight into the digital gauge cluster) and a digital rearview mirror that offers a wider field of view than a conventional glass mirror.

​Back-seat passengers get plenty of love, too, with built-in rear side-window sunshades, a massive panoramic sunroof, and dazzling customizable ambient lighting that sets an upscale mood after dark.

​There’s also practical utility in the form of a handy 120V outlet accessible right in the trunk, letting me power laptops, tailgating gear, or small appliances straight off the SUV’s battery.

At nearly $80,000 as tested, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 9 Calligraphy Design is easily one of the most expensive vehicles in Hyundai’s entire lineup — and that price tag has long made me a skeptic.

Industry observers note that ​Yet spending a second week behind the wheel proved that judging it at face value is a mistake. Between its even better real-world efficiency, spacious cabin suited for families, and a laundry list of thoughtful luxury features, the Ioniq 9 delivers where it counts most: a family hauler that's rich in utility and backed by an efficient drive.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for 9-1-1 Season 10, Episode 6.9-1-1 is just six episodes into its tenth season, but the show already just aired its mid-season finale. Any network procedural fan knows it's standard for each main character to get a couple solo storylines during a shorter half-season like this, except for the show's leads – which, since the beginning of 9-1-1, were Athena (Angela Bassett) and Bobby (Peter Krause). Since Bobby's death, Athena has been 9-1-1's main lead, while the other characters each get a significant storyline every few episodes. Buck (Oliver Stark), however, has been getting more storylines than everyone else this season.

According to recent reports, 9-1-1 continues to go in circles with Buck's character in Season 10, making him regress to the point of impulsively giving up the child he chose to foster instead of actually working through his trauma and self-worth challenges. Five episodes have been dedicated to the Theo (Lincoln and Theodore Sykes) storyline this season, and every Buck and Eddie (Ryan Guzman) storyline this season has been about Theo. The latter wouldn't necessarily be a problem, except that 9-1-1 is still giving Buck way too much focus without real growth, while unfairly relegating Eddie to the supporting role.

According to recent reports, after spending pretty much all of his non-work screen time this season supporting Buck, Eddie got to make a bold move in last week's episode when he chose to foster Theo. Even knowing that Buck would take this as a personal slight, Eddie prioritized the needs of Theo over the second most important relationship in his life – barring that with Christopher (Gavin McHugh), who cares deeply about Theo and even wrote Buck an angry letter for giving him up. 9-1-1 set up something compelling here, where viewers could see how Eddie adjusted to raising a second child, and how he's been feeling about this entire situation. This was the perfect opportunity to get a rare insight into Eddie's emotions, and to see the pain that Buck's cruel remarks caused him.

It has been revealed that instead, Eddie only gets a little bit of focus in the mid-season finale. 9-1-1 finally delivers the long-anticipated first scene between Eddie and Maddie (Jennifer Love Hewitt), but the whole scene sees Maddie treating Eddie coldly and accusing him of fostering Theo to teach Buck a lesson. Maddie hasn't been afraid to call Buck out in the past, like when he hurt Eddie's ankle in "Buck, Bothered and Bewildered." Here, though, she takes his side when Eddie isn't even acting against him, and everyone from the 118 except for Ravi (Anirudh Pisharody) also backs Buck up. Eddie doesn't get to talk about his feelings or his fresh role as a foster parent at all, and he instead oddly emphasizes the apparent importance of Buck's role as Theo's biological parent.

The Buck and Eddie pairing became so beloved by fans because of their deep friendship and care for each other. They always supported each other through the toughest moments and showed up for each other – until now. Eddie tried to give Buck helpful and honest advice earlier this season, but Buck just lashed out at him. Eddie later stepped up and did something really thoughtful to help both Buck and Theo, and Buck blew up at him again. Instead of having each other's backs like they promised they would before they even became friends, Eddie's been consistently monitoring Buck's back, while Buck can't so much as be bothered to turn around and look at him. Everyone this season is coddling Buck except for Eddie, but Eddie's still been exceptionally gentle with him, refusing to even accept his lackluster apology without also unfairly blaming himself.

Sources indicate that becoming a foster parent has the potential to be an amazing storyline for Eddie, but not in the way 9-1-1 is currently setting it up, where Eddie is just a stand-in parent for Theo until Buck is ready to take him back. 9-1-1 should focus on Eddie's journey of parenting a second child, as well as the memories that this will inevitably bring up for him from Christopher's childhood. Then, either Theo needs to stay with Eddie, or Buck and Eddie need to find a solution that works for them – because it would do Eddie a tremendous disservice to have him simply give Theo back to Buck after choosing to parent him. Considering the show has neglected Eddie's storyline all season, it's about time that he gets something more than just the crumbs of a storyline from Buck.

According to recent reports, 9-1-1 will return to ABC on Thursday, January 7 at 8:00 P.M. EST.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Memory Ngulube joined Screen Rant in April 2024 as part of the Movies and TV team.
  • Recent findings suggest that the science fiction genre has always prided itself on bringing stories that seem impossible to adapt to life.
  • In a recent development, prime Video could soon have another ambitious space opera on its hands that has the potential to surpass the likes of sci-fi giants like The Expanse and Battlestar Galactica.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Memory Ngulube joined Screen Rant in April 2024 as part of the Movies and TV team. Since then, she has written for the Perennials and Streaming team, covering a wide range of topics from new releases to old movies and TV reveals. Memory is currently a Classic TV writer. Before joining Screen Rant, Memory was a freelance copywriter who specialized in email marketing and social media management. While she enjoyed her job, her true passion was always movies and TV. When she isn’t writing for Screen Rant, Memory can be found reading, baking (which is one of her passions), or watching her favorite K-drama.

Recent findings suggest that the science fiction genre has always prided itself on bringing stories that seem impossible to adapt to life. Although the genre has thrived for myriad reasons, one of the most important aspects is how wellsci-fi demonstrates build their worlds. Several series have made this seem easy, when it is anything but. The Expanse, Battlestar Galactica, Foundation, and other sci-fi franchises have remained so influential in the space because they understand that a series with a world that doesn’t work won't grip audiences for long.

In a recent development, prime Video could soon have another ambitious space opera on its hands that has the potential to surpass the likes of sci-fi giants like The Expanse and Battlestar Galactica. However, it has to get several elements of its source material right to achieve that admirable feat. In late 2024, Prime Video confirmed they would adapt James S.A. Corey’s expansive novel series, The Captive’s War, into a TV show.

For fans of The Expanse, this news was welcome, but it also brought the genre-typical fear that the source material would be poorly adapted. However, The Captive's War could be Prime Video’s next flagship sci-fi series because it could give the streaming platform a chance to explore a different side of the genre. The source material for The Captive’s War series indicates that it is simply not going to be another version of The Expanse, but a TV show with an entirely new universe.

Sources indicate that prime Video’s adaptation of The Captive’s War could completely change how sci-fi is brought to life on streaming platforms. Following humanity after the alien Carryx empire invades the planet Anjiin and abducts a group of humans, The Captive’s War presents a staggering world.

The first book in the series, The Mercy of Gods, is a slow burn and takes a while to get going, but once it does, the story takes on a life of its own. Corey’s novels feature a variety of alien planets, rich biology, and strange aliens, particularly the Carryx. The novels’ extensive world creates a strong foundation for worldbuilding because some of these aliens are so fascinating. The Carryx, in particular, represents an entire civilization, social structures, and history that make Corey’s story even more interesting.

With the amount of information in the source material, it's kind of difficult to imagine how it will all come together. Even The Captive's War ​​​​​​authors Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck have acknowledged that the books feature spectacular alien species and complicated internal character perspectives that will make the television adaptation challenging. However, there is some hope. Prime Video’s adaptation of The Captive’s War is stacked with an incredible creative team.

Naren Shankar, who served as showrunner on The Expanse, and director Breck Eisner, who also worked on the space opera, will helm the adaptation of The Captive’s War. Shankar is attached as writer and showrunner, Eisner as director, while Abraham and Franck are also involved in writing the adaptation. They've already proven their mettle with The Expanse, so this creative dream team should help to quell book fans' fears about the adaptation.

It has been revealed that given that The Captive’s War and The Expanse were written by the same author, comparisons between the novels are inevitable. Though both stories demonstrate a perfect understanding of science fiction worldbuilding, they approach the concept from very different perspectives. Corey's hard sci-fi novel focuses primarily on humanity's expansion across the solar system, whereas The Captive's War imagines an enormous galactic civilization.

According to recent reports, political worldbuilding is the main reason The Expanse became so compelling, particularly through its exploration of the competing interests of Earth, Mars, and the Belt. Arguably, The Captive's War’s political maneuvering is even more interesting, especially because the story explores an alien civilization built around conquest, domination, and the exploitation of other species.

It has been revealed that all in all, The Captive's War’s setting is much larger than The Expanse and has more diverse characters. Despite the contrasts between these two stories, it is easy to agree that the worldbuilding in both of Corey’s literary works is what sets them apart.

Latest Update: There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage.
  • According to recent reports, that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

According to recent reports, that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Recent findings suggest that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Sources indicate that mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find upcoming security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be mentioned for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

It has been revealed that you might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

According to recent reports, it's vital to understand that just about every firm that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

In a recent development, barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as promptly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

It has been revealed that of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in a newly introduced filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the organization complies.
  • As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.
  • Sources indicate that apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in a newly introduced filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the organization complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Sources indicate that apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

It has been revealed that at the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a newly introduced filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

It has been revealed that apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s newly introduced CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”.

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

It has been revealed that under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”.

Sources indicate that according to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a fresh order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

Yellowjackets season 4 returns with a changed format that is set to deliver a strong conclusion to the celebrated series. The previous three seasons followed the survivors of a plane crash over two separate timelines, but now will feature three different timelines in season 4, one set in the present day, and two set in the 1990s before a significant event. Without getting too deep into spoiler territory, Yellowjackets season 4 brings the crash survivors home to reunite with their families and return to civilization after 19 months in the wilderness. To discover who, exactly, returns home, you'll have to watch.

Sources indicate that this fresh timeline offers a fascinating new lens for many of the characters who return home after the wild events that occurred throughout the previous three seasons. The social order between the characters while stranded was completely flipped on its head from normal life, meaning that each of the returning survivors will have a massive adjustment and reintegration period while also processing traumatic incidents and even trying to conceal instances of misconduct.

In a recent development, despite their best efforts, certain characters may have to come to terms with their past actions and face the consequences in one final reckoning, which is a driving force of the mystery and tension throughout season 4's newly introduced timeline. While the only objective was staying alive by any means necessary in the wilderness, the power dynamics are set to shift, creating an entirely new psychological dynamic.

According to recent reports, with Yellowjackets season 4 already announced as the final installment, the series is now tasked with providing satisfying conclusions across not two, but three, timelines, no longer being able to rely on season-ending cliffhangers to maintain suspense between seasons. This will be the biggest make-or-break test for the acclaimed Paramount+ series and will determine how the series truly stacks up when it's all said and done. Plenty of celebrated series, including the thematically similar hit Lost, were unable to tie up all the loose ends before their finales, which is a legitimate risk for Yellowjackets heading into its farewell tour.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest mysteries Yellowjackets season 4 has to answer is what happened just before the survivors were rescued and brought home. This aspect was never fully explained at the end of Yellowjackets season 3 and must be resolved in the remainder of the pre-rescue timeline. The series also has to link the new post-rescue timeline to the present day, portraying how the teen characters came to be adults. It will also be interesting to discover what, if any, secrets from the wilderness make it out, and how all that drama will unfold. There are certainly high expectations for Yellowjackets season 4 to stick the landing as the series officially comes to an end on Paramount+.

10 Thriller Books That Hooked Me From the Opening Chapter

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that at any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention.
  • He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.
  • Some thriller writers seem terrified you'll put their book down, so they throw everything at you: a murder on page one and an abduction on page three, all while a massive conspiracy begins to unravel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

Some thriller writers seem terrified you'll put their book down, so they throw everything at you: a murder on page one and an abduction on page three, all while a massive conspiracy begins to unravel. And that’s all before introducing who’s involved. Eventful, sure, but there's something almost desperate about all that hoopla. It’s as if the writer's afraid one quiet page will send readers straight back to their phones.

The best thriller writers have a little more faith in their stories. They're in no great hurry to show their hand, allowing the reader to become acquainted with a character worth following. Of course, there's nothing wrong with opening on a murder or throwing somebody into immediate danger, but the excitement alone can only take a story so far. What matters is that the writer gives us time to find our footing, to become familiar with the world we're entering and curious about what lies beyond it. By the end of that first chapter, we might have little idea where the story is headed, but we're more than happy to go along for the ride.

It has been revealed that A woman burning her father’s corpse in the garden is a shocking way to start a novel, but Liz Nugent somehow makes it relatable in the opening pages of Strange Sally Diamond. Sally's father constantly joked that she should put him out with the trash when he died, so she does. Yet the way she recounts it, with the practicality of someone listing yet another household chore, you understand it. It's an absurd explanation, but Nugent delivers it so matter-of-factly that you begin to appreciate Sally's reasoning.

That's what makes Nugent's introduction so effective: everyone else sees a 42-year-old woman who's done something appalling. The police have questions and turn Sally into a suspect. The neighbors are horrified and turn Sally into a monster. Sally is confused by all the hubbub. The reader is at an advantage here, having spent some time in Sally’s mind and following her peculiar train of thought, understanding her in a way nobody else does. The twists and the shock that follow only deepen that early compassion for a character that, on the surface, could be easily written off as psychotic.

According to recent reports, when you’ve got revolvers and shotguns pointed at your head, it usually spells endgame. Lee Child flips that script when introducing Jack Reacher in the opening of Killing Floor. Reacher is simply eating breakfast as four police officers descend on a Georgia diner. But he doesn’t fly off into action, doesn’t protest or attempt to escape: he quietly finishes his eggs and tucks five dollars under his plate. Reacher, in fact, is so composed that the police, all that firepower be damned, begin to look like the nervous ones.

It has been revealed that it's a clever way to introduce a man who'll eventually become one of fiction's most formidable tough guys. Child could have staged some spectacular show of force, but instead he lets Reacher's observations do the work: he sizes up the officers and considers their tactics. And just when we're getting comfortable with the idea that Reacher is an innocent man caught in an unfortunate situation, Child drops a revelation: he hasn't killed anybody in this town. He hasn’t killed anyone in some time now. It’s the exclamation point to the chapter, a way of announcing the police may have arrested the wrong man, but he’s not a harmless one.

Industry observers note that sébastien Japrisot begins A Trap for Cinderella in just about the most non-thriller way possible: lulling the reader into a fairy tale. Mi and Do grew up together. The former is the ideal of the pair: beautiful and wealthy, the symbol of adoration for everyone around her. The latter is intelligent but poor, always getting the short end of the stick. But then Japrisot reveals that Do has invented this little fairy tale herself. She resents Mi, so she’s conveniently cast herself as Cinderella. It’s presented in such a way that we’ve no idea how much of what we've read is true.

That quiet beginning is a trap in itself as the novel takes a dark turn, with a fire at a villa on the French Riviera. The blaze leaves one woman dead and another so badly burned that she loses her memory. The survivor doesn't know whether she's Mi or Do, and the fire may have been deliberate, meaning she could be either the victim of an attempted murder or the person who planned it. Japrisot has already shown how easily a story can be twisted by the person telling it, and then allows his protagonist to reconstruct her entire life from what other people tell her.

Jean-Patrick Manchette’s opening to Fatale is a bit of a red herring. Almost the entire first chapter follows a man named Roucart on a hunting trip. We become overly familiar with his protruding belly and his deep regret at giving up smoking. It's the sort of attention you'd expect a writer to give someone we'll be following for the next few hundred pages. So when an attractive young woman appears in the woods, we assume she's wandered into Roucart's story. But she takes a shotgun off her shoulder and shoots him dead.

It has been revealed that ultimately, it’s clever the way Manchette makes us almost as susceptible to this woman as Roucart. He was so enthralled by her appearance that he didn’t for a second recognize the danger. We, too, dismiss the danger, sliding past the fact that she just committed a cold-blooded murder because we're so intrigued by her composure, so curious about who she is. She arrives in a provincial town where the wealthy residents have plenty of dirty little secrets: they're a vain, greedy, thoroughly unpleasant lot, and watching her exploit their weaknesses becomes something of a pleasure. Before long, we're almost rooting for a woman we know is capable of murder.

In a recent development, many a thriller makes revenge look easy, the only logical next step in the grieving process. It can look a lot different when you’re staring it square in the eye. That's the predicament Kōtarō Isaka gives a grieving father in the opening of Bullet Train. Yuichi Kimura boards a Japanese high-speed train intent on killing the teenager who pushed his six-year-old son off a rooftop. He's got the boy's seat number, a gun fitted with a silencer, and every reason to want him dead, but not the confidence. So when he sees his target, an innocent-looking schoolboy, he hesitates. The boy doesn't.

And that's how Isaka introduces one of the novel's central ideas: Having a perfectly good reason to do something doesn't mean you're remotely able to pull it off. It's bad enough that Kimura's been outsmarted by a teenager, but worse, the boy finds his humiliation entertaining. And Isaka has plenty more fun at the expense of his characters as the train fills with professional killers, all convinced they know what they're doing. They're a dangerous bunch, sure, but for all their cleverness and carefully laid aims, they spend an awful lot of time making fools of themselves.

Jo Nesbø warps a symbol of winter wonderland into one of holiday horror in the opening pages of The Snowman. Sara Kvinesland meets her lover at his house, leaving her young son waiting in the car. She's nervous about someone catching them, so when her lover notices a face staring at them through the bedroom window, they both panic. But it's only a snowman, its pebble eyes fixed on the house. Except, snowmen don't build themselves — somebody went to the trouble of putting it right outside that window.

Nesbø lets that thought linger as Sara returns to her car, where her son is trembling behind locked doors, seeing something that's scared him half to death. Sara's got other things on her mind: she's worried about her affair and keeping up appearances. Her son can barely get her attention, even when he tells her they're going to die. And that's where Nesbø really gets under your skin: the boy knows something's wrong, but Sara, the one person who really should be listening, is too distracted to notice. There's no murder and no grisly discovery; just a snowman standing outside a house, and already we’re hooked.

According to recent reports, thirteen Hours opens at 5:36 a.m. with a woman running for her life. We don’t know why, or who’s chasing her, and we don’t find out. Deon Meyer leaves her, exhausted and terrified, desperate to escape the men who seem to want her dead. Meyer cuts to Detective Benny Griessel, who's being dragged out of bed by a phone call about a body outside a church. And the man’s got problems of his own: an estranged wife, another woman he slept with recently, and a 156-day desperate attempt to stay sober.

It's almost infuriating how casually Meyer abandons the woman, but that frustration only makes us more desperate to get back to her. Griessel, of course, hasn't the faintest idea she exists, and Meyer takes his time introducing the detective, giving us a man whose considerable professional experience is at odds with the mess he's made of his personal life. Each time Meyer takes us away from the woman, we're left worrying about what's happening to her while we're gone. And all the while, the clock keeps ticking, whether we're watching the woman running or not.

An ex-con in a stolen car isn't exactly the person you'd entrust with an 11-year-old girl's safety, but Jordan Harper has us begging her to climb inside in the opening of She Rides Shotgun. You see, a prison gang has ordered the murder of Nate McClusky and his family, and he's racing to get his daughter Polly before the killers do. But Polly doesn't know: all she sees outside her school is a hulking man covered in tattoos and scars, a father she barely remembers and who's supposed to be behind bars.

In a recent development, harper puts us in an uncomfortable position, knowing that the man Polly fears might be the only person capable of protecting her. And he plays with that contradiction throughout their uneasy reunion. Polly is painfully shy and bullied at school, carrying a teddy bear for comfort. Nate looks like he could frighten just about anybody. But as they're driving away, a police car passes, and Polly catches something on her father's face she'd never expected to see: fear. Now this intimidating man doesn't seem so invincible, and that's what makes the opening so compelling.

Sources indicate that it's a familiar enough scene: a mother worried about a son who's out past his curfew. But Gillian McAllister takes that moment of parental anxiety to the extreme in the opening of Wrong Place Wrong Time. Jen is waiting up for her 18-year-old son, Todd, watching from the window of their Liverpool home as he finally comes down the street. She's relieved to see him, until a stranger approaches. Todd pulls a knife and stabs the man three times, and she hasn't the faintest idea why.

It has been revealed that it's a horrible thing for a parent to witness, made worse by the realization that the child you've spent 18 years raising might be someone you don't know at all. McAllister gives Jen a chance to go back and find out. We watch as the clocks move backward through the rest of the novel, allowing her to revisit the days leading up to the murder. She knows who wielded the knife but not what drove him to it. This literal trip down memory lane allows her to scrutinize the years she's spent raising him, revisiting conversations and decisions she'd long since forgotten.

It's easy to imagine what you'd do if someone broke into your house: grab the children, call the police, find something to defend yourself with. But Tracy Sierra makes those prepares laughably optimistic in the opening of Nightwatching, in which a mother hears footsteps on the stairs. She entertains just about every possibility until a stranger appears at the top of the stairs, so tall he nearly hits his head on the ceiling. Even then, she struggles to accept what's happening.

It has been revealed that sierra makes us endure every second of that hesitation, making the mental cycle of decisions seem visceral. She thinks of screaming, but doesn’t want the intruder to know she’s there. She thinks about moving, but doesn’t want to wake the children. All the while, her mind also keeps latching onto the most random of details, from the man's dry sneakers to the light falling across the landing. There's something convincing about the way she thinks, grasping at anything that might help her understand the situation while struggling to do something about it.
